m1.title: Month 1 — External Financial Reporting Decisions (CMA P1-A)
m1.description: The 4 statements, recognition & measurement, revenue/expense, disclosures — built from a realistic construction GL.

weeks.title: The Four Financial Statements & Articulation (CMA P1-A · feeds FAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — two balanced ledgers are not one company

Real MBG control totals: the MBG general ledger is $12,480,000.00 and the Riverton general ledger is $16,920,000.00; both were reported as balanced in the Q1 close analysis. Those figures are control evidence, not permission to combine the entities. MBG and Riverton have different bank accounts, reciprocal intercompany accounts, and separate reporting responsibilities. Before preparing any statement, select one entity, one reporting date, one accounting basis, and one exact trial balance.

A balanced trial balance proves that posted debits equal posted credits. It does not prove that accounts are correctly classified, that all transactions were recorded, or that the reporting period is closed. MBG's Q1 remained open with 12 items even though the ledgers balanced. Financial statement preparation therefore begins with the adjusted trial balance and ends with articulation checks across four statements.

Concept — four views of one accounting system

The balance sheet reports assets, liabilities, and equity at a point in time. Its governing equation is Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Cash, receivables, and construction in progress are assets because they represent controlled resources with expected future benefit. Accounts payable, retainage payable, and notes payable are liabilities because they are present obligations. Equity is the residual interest.

The income statement reports revenues, expenses, gains, and losses over a period. Net income measures performance under accrual accounting; it is not the change in cash. Construction revenue can be recognized before billing or collection, while equipment purchases may use cash without becoming immediate expense.

The statement of changes in equity reconciles beginning equity to ending equity. For a simple corporation: Beginning retained earnings + net income − dividends = ending retained earnings. Additional paid-in capital, owner contributions, distributions, and accumulated other comprehensive income appear when applicable. A closing entry transfers temporary-account results into retained earnings; it does not create the underlying profit.

The statement of cash flows explains the change in cash through operating, investing, and financing activities. Under the indirect method, operating cash flow begins with net income and adjusts for noncash items and changes in operating assets and liabilities. Buying equipment is generally investing; borrowing principal is financing; interest classification follows the applicable reporting framework and policy.

Articulation checkpoints

  • Ending cash on the cash-flow statement equals balance-sheet cash.
  • Net income flows from the income statement into retained earnings, subject to dividends and other equity changes.
  • Ending retained earnings equals the equity statement and balance sheet.
  • Every balance-sheet account derives from the adjusted trial balance.
  • The cash-flow change plus beginning cash equals ending cash.

Worked example — build all four statements

The following compact trial balance is illustrative; the real MBG and Riverton totals above are control totals, but the source does not provide a complete account-by-account adjusted TB suitable for publication here.

AccountDebitCredit
Cash$180,000—
Accounts receivable$260,000—
WIP/CIP$420,000—
Equipment, net$140,000—
Accounts payable—$220,000
Debt—$300,000
Common stock—$200,000
Beginning retained earnings—$120,000
Revenue—$600,000
Cost of revenue$420,000—
Operating expense$20,000—
Total$1,440,000$1,440,000

The income statement reports $600,000 revenue minus $420,000 cost of revenue minus $20,000 operating expense, producing illustrative net income of $160,000. With no dividends in the displayed trial balance, ending retained earnings are $120,000 + $160,000 = $280,000.

The balance sheet reports assets of $1,000,000: cash $180,000, receivables $260,000, WIP $420,000, and net equipment $140,000. Liabilities are $520,000 and ending equity is $480,000: common stock $200,000 plus retained earnings $280,000. Liabilities plus equity equal $1,000,000. The closing process removes the temporary revenue and expense accounts while transferring their $160,000 net result into retained earnings.

Assume beginning cash was an illustrative $110,000. Cash increased $70,000. One possible cash-flow reconciliation is $90,000 operating inflow, $50,000 equipment purchase, and $30,000 financing inflow: $90,000 − $50,000 + $30,000 = $70,000. Under the indirect method, operating cash flow would begin with $160,000 net income and explain the $70,000 net reduction from noncash and working-capital adjustments to reach $90,000 operating cash.

The point is not to reverse-engineer cash from a desired answer. Each change must be supported by comparative balance sheets and transaction detail. The articulation equations then detect omissions: if cash-flow ending cash is $175,000 while the balance sheet shows $180,000, the package has a $5,000 unresolved error.

Apply the method to MBG

  1. Export the MBG adjusted TB from JCS for the exact cutoff; do not call JCS Ledgerline 100.
  2. Compute true ending balances from beginning plus YTD debits minus YTD credits because “Acct Ending Bal” is not cumulative.
  3. Map exact accounts to statement lines; never use substring matches.
  4. Prepare the income statement and equity rollforward before finalizing the balance sheet.
  5. Build the cash-flow statement from comparative balances and supported noncash details.
  6. Run articulation checks and document every difference to $0.00.
  7. Repeat independently for Riverton; consolidation is a later layer with eliminations.

A bank tie is stronger evidence for cash than an internally balanced GL. MBG account 102.1 must tie to its First Regional Bank statement, while Riverton account 102 ties to its own statement. Entity segregation is an assertion about ownership, not merely presentation.

Common construction-package traps

Classifying WIP as current does not mean it is cash-equivalent. It must be evaluated within the operating cycle and supported by job detail. A large contract asset is not the same as accounts receivable because the right may remain conditional on something other than time. Retainage can also require separate presentation or disclosure depending on the facts. These distinctions affect current ratio, working capital, and cash-flow analysis even when total assets are unchanged.

Contra accounts must remain connected to their related assets. Accumulated depreciation reduces property and equipment; an allowance reduces the related receivable. Netting unrelated debit and credit balances can make a trial balance appear concise while violating presentation rules. Likewise, offsetting intercompany accounts belongs to consolidation after reciprocity is proved, not to the separate MBG or Riverton statements.

Comparative statements add another control. Each ending balance becomes the next period's beginning balance, subject to supported retrospective adjustments. If opening retained earnings does not equal the prior issued ending balance, identify the restatement, prior-period correction, or data error explicitly. Never plug the difference into current income.

Finally, distinguish transactions from classifications. Paying AP changes cash and a liability but not current expense. Depreciation changes expense and a contra asset without using cash. Closing a home transfers WIP to cost of sales and recognizes the related balance-sheet relief. Every event must appear consistently across the statements it affects.

CPA Crossover — FAR

FAR adds classification, disclosure, and presentation detail: current versus noncurrent, discontinued operations, other comprehensive income, noncash financing and investing disclosures, and statement format. The same articulation logic remains central. A question may provide comparative balance sheets and an income statement, then require cash flows; solve by identifying account changes, classifying their causes, and excluding noncash transactions from the main cash-flow sections.

Practice and recap

When reviewing a package, ask four separate questions: does the balance sheet balance, does the income statement reflect the period, does equity roll correctly, and does cash reconcile to independent evidence? Then ask whether all four agree with one another. A balanced statement can still be wrong; articulation makes separate errors collide.

Recap: the four statements are not independent reports. Net income changes equity, transactions change balance-sheet accounts, and the cash-flow statement explains one balance-sheet change. Start from an adjusted, entity-specific trial balance and require exact articulation before relying on any total.

flashcards.front: What does a balanced trial balance prove?
flashcards.back: Only that posted debits equal posted credits; it does not prove completeness, cutoff, valuation, or classification.

flashcards.front: What is the balance-sheet equation?
flashcards.back: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.

flashcards.front: How does net income articulate with equity?
flashcards.back: Net income increases retained earnings, subject to dividends, distributions, and other equity changes.

flashcards.front: What must ending cash on the cash-flow statement equal?
flashcards.back: The balance-sheet cash balance for the same entity and date.

flashcards.front: Why can net income differ from operating cash flow?
flashcards.back: Accruals, noncash expenses, and working-capital changes separate performance recognition from cash timing.

flashcards.front: What are the real MBG and Riverton GL control totals?
flashcards.back: MBG $12,480,000.00 and Riverton $16,920,000.00; keep the entities separate.

flashcards.front: Which statement reconciles beginning to ending retained earnings?
flashcards.back: The statement of changes in equity.

flashcards.front: What is the strongest evidence for a bank balance?
flashcards.back: The bank statement and reconciliation, not merely a balanced GL.

questions.q: Illustrative revenue is $600,000, cost of revenue $420,000, and operating expense $20,000. Net income is:
Beginning retained earnings are $120,000, net income is $160,000, and dividends are $30,000. Ending retained earnings are:
Which event is generally an investing cash flow?
questions.explain: Purchasing a long-lived asset is generally an investing activity.

questions.q: A trial balance is balanced. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.explain: Arithmetic equality does not establish the other financial-statement assertions.

questions.q: Ending cash per the cash-flow statement is $175,000 and balance-sheet cash is $180,000. What should happen?
choices: Investigate and resolve the $5,000 articulation error
questions.explain: The statements must articulate for the same entity and date; an unexplained difference is an error.

questions.q: Which statement reports financial position at a point in time?
questions.explain: The balance sheet presents assets, liabilities, and equity at the reporting date.

questions.q: Why must MBG and Riverton statements be prepared separately first?
choices: They are distinct entities with separate accounts and ownership assertions
questions.explain: Entity-specific ledgers and bank accounts must be correct before any consolidation layer.

weeks.title: Asset & Liability Recognition and Measurement (CMA P1-A · feeds FAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — $14 million is an asset, not an expense

Real MBG balances: MBG carries $14,480,000.00 and Riverton carries $11,360,000.00 in the 14xxxxx WIP/job-cost account series. The entities remain separate. These balances represent construction in progress: resources consumed to create homes or projects that have not yet closed. Recording every job cost as immediate expense would understate assets and distort period margin; leaving completed or impaired projects in WIP would overstate assets.

Recognition asks whether an item belongs on the financial statements. Measurement asks at what amount. Classification asks where and for how long. Each question requires evidence; a job code alone cannot turn a corporate period cost into an asset.

Concept — recognition before measurement

An asset is a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events. A liability is a present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events. Equity is residual. Revenue and expense recognition describe changes in assets and liabilities other than owner transactions.

Historical cost is often the initial measurement basis because it is transaction-based and verifiable. Subsequent measurement may involve amortized cost, depreciation, impairment, lower-of-cost tests, present value, or fair value depending on the item and applicable guidance. The CMA exam expects you to distinguish measurement attributes and understand their effect on statements and ratios.

WIP capitalization boundary

Direct materials, direct labor, subcontract costs, and allocable production overhead can enter WIP when they relate to construction activity and satisfy the applicable capitalization policy. Abnormal waste, unsupported rework, selling costs, and unrelated corporate administration generally do not become assets merely because they are charged to a job. The cost must contribute to the resource or contract activity and be recoverable under the relevant accounting model.

A WIP rollforward is Beginning WIP + eligible additions ± supported reclasses − transfers on close = ending WIP. Job-level detail must reconcile to exact GL accounts. JCS's “Acct Ending Bal” is not cumulative, so true ending balance is beginning balance plus YTD debits minus YTD credits.

Liability recognition boundary

Accounts payable arises when goods or services have been received and an obligation exists, even if the invoice has not arrived. An accrued liability records the obligation using a reasonable estimate. Retainage payable remains an obligation despite delayed payment. Debt is measured and classified using its contractual terms. A contingent loss is recognized or disclosed according to likelihood and estimability under applicable guidance; management preference does not control.

Worked example — classify one construction purchase

Assume MBG receives an illustrative $120,000 framing subcontract invoice for an active home. Ten percent is contractually retained, and the work is approved before period end. The full $120,000 is an eligible job cost. The entry is:

AccountDebitCredit
WIP — subcontract cost$120,000—
Trade AP currently due—$108,000
Retainage payable—$12,000

The holdback changes payment timing, not incurred cost. Recording only $108,000 in WIP understates both the asset and liability by $12,000. Paying $108,000 later debits AP and credits cash; it does not create expense. Releasing the $12,000 later settles retainage and does not record the job cost twice.

Now assume illustrative corporate advertising of $15,000 was miscoded to the same job. Advertising does not become construction WIP through coding. Correct the classification by crediting WIP and debiting advertising expense. Total assets and current-period profit each decrease $15,000. This is a financial-account reclass, unlike a same-account job reclass that changes only the job dimension.

Measurement and estimate changes

Suppose an illustrative piece of equipment costs $100,000, has a $10,000 residual value, and a five-year useful life. Straight-line annual depreciation is ($100,000 − $10,000) ÷ 5 = $18,000. The asset remains at $100,000 gross cost while accumulated depreciation grows; net carrying amount falls. Depreciation is allocation, not valuation.

If facts later indicate that a recorded asset is not recoverable under its applicable impairment model, perform the required test and recognize any loss. Do not leave stale WIP because removing it would hurt margin. Conversely, do not write down an asset solely because one manager dislikes a project. Recognition and measurement rely on current evidence and the applicable standard.

Present value is important for long-term obligations. An illustrative $110,000 payment due in one year at a 10% market rate has a present value of $100,000. Initial liability measurement at present value produces $10,000 of interest accretion over the year, subject to the specific guidance and transaction terms.

Cutoff, current classification, and assertions

Cutoff determines whether the resource or obligation existed at period end. A vendor invoice dated after year-end may still relate to work received before year-end and require accrual. A check issued before year-end does not eliminate a liability if it was voided or never delivered under the governing facts. The bank tie, receiving evidence, contract terms, and subsequent-disbursement review are stronger than invoice date alone.

Current classification generally depends on expected realization, consumption, or settlement within the operating cycle or one year, subject to applicable rules. Construction operating cycles can exceed a year, so mechanical use of twelve months can misclassify working-capital accounts. Disclose significant policies and judgments when users need them to understand measurement.

Close procedure for real MBG WIP

  1. Reconcile exact 14xxxxx accounts to the MBG job ledger at the same cutoff.
  2. Test additions to invoices, payroll, receiving evidence, approval, and entity.
  3. Review negative, stale, closed, or no-job balances.
  4. Separate eligible production cost from period expense and abnormal items.
  5. Verify transfers for homes that closed and retain current active-job costs.
  6. Assess recoverability and estimates without hiding unfavorable information.
  7. Repeat independently for Riverton's fictionalized $11,360,000.00 balance.

Measurement decision matrix

For each balance, document four layers. First, identify the unit of account: one invoice, one asset, one job, or a portfolio as permitted. Second, establish initial measurement from transaction evidence and directly attributable costs. Third, identify the subsequent model—depreciation, amortization, impairment, present value accretion, fair value, or settlement. Fourth, determine presentation and disclosure, including current classification and significant estimates.

Consider an illustrative $50,000 material purchase received for an active job before cutoff. If title and control transferred and the material is eligible, debit WIP or inventory and credit AP even when the invoice arrives later. If the material remains at a supplier and MBG lacks control, do not recognize it merely because a purchase order exists. If it was damaged through abnormal handling, evaluate whether the loss belongs in current expense rather than WIP. The same dollar amount can therefore produce different accounting because the underlying rights and events differ.

Measurement uncertainty does not excuse omission. Use the best supportable estimate, disclose significant uncertainty when required, and revise estimates prospectively when facts change. An error is different: using information that was available but applied incorrectly may require correction rather than prospective estimate treatment. The close memo should state which conclusion applies and why.

CPA Crossover — FAR

FAR tests recognition and measurement item by item: inventory, property and equipment, contingencies, debt, present value, impairment, and classification. The construction hook does not replace the guidance. Identify the unit of account, initial basis, subsequent model, and required presentation. On simulations, reconcile the rollforward and post adjustments that preserve debits, credits, and statement classification.

Practice and recap

For any proposed asset, ask: what resource is controlled, what past event created it, what future benefit is expected, which costs are eligible, and what subsequent measurement applies? For any liability, ask: what present obligation exists, when was it created, what must be transferred, and how reliably can it be measured?

Recap: WIP is an asset because eligible construction costs create or enhance a controlled resource or contract-related asset. It is not a parking lot. Full incurred obligations are recorded despite retainage, completed costs transfer out, and unsupported or impaired amounts are corrected promptly.

flashcards.front: What is an asset?
flashcards.back: A present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events.

flashcards.front: What is a liability?
flashcards.back: A present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events.

flashcards.front: What are the real MBG and Riverton WIP balances?
flashcards.back: MBG $14,480,000.00 and Riverton $11,360,000.00; they remain separate.

flashcards.front: Does retainage reduce the amount of incurred subcontract cost?
flashcards.back: No. Record full eligible cost and split the obligation between current AP and retainage payable.

flashcards.front: What is the WIP rollforward?
flashcards.back: Beginning WIP + eligible additions ± supported reclasses − transfers on close = ending WIP.

flashcards.front: Is depreciation a process of valuation?
flashcards.back: No. It systematically allocates depreciable cost over useful life.

flashcards.front: Can a job code make advertising an asset?
flashcards.back: No. Recognition follows economic substance and applicable guidance, not coding.

flashcards.front: Why review subsequent disbursements?
flashcards.back: They can reveal liabilities for goods or services received before the reporting cutoff.

questions.q: An illustrative $120,000 approved subcontract invoice has 10% retainage. What eligible WIP cost is recorded?
questions.explain: The full service has been received; $108,000 is current AP and $12,000 is retainage payable.

questions.q: Illustrative equipment costs $100,000, residual value is $10,000, and useful life is five years. Annual straight-line depreciation is:
Which cost is least likely to qualify for construction WIP?
questions.explain: Advertising is generally a period cost unrelated to creating the construction asset.

questions.q: A $110,000 payment due in one year discounted at 10% has what illustrative present value?
A vendor invoice arrives after year-end for work completed before year-end. The best response is:
choices: Ignore it because the invoice is late
Evaluate and accrue the period-end obligation
questions.explain: Receipt of goods or services and the resulting obligation—not invoice arrival alone—drives cutoff.

questions.q: What happens when a home closes and its eligible accumulated cost leaves WIP?
choices: It generally transfers to cost of sales under the applicable model
questions.explain: The asset is relieved and matched with the related sale rather than remaining in active WIP.

questions.q: Which statement about measurement is correct?
choices: All assets remain at historical cost forever
Subsequent measurement depends on the item and applicable guidance
questions.explain: Different assets use depreciation, amortized cost, impairment, fair value, or other prescribed models.

weeks.title: Revenue & Expense Recognition — ASC 606 Foundations (CMA P1-A · feeds FAR/BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — progress is an accounting estimate, not a billing percentage

Real MBG structure: the Global Status Report supplies project progress evidence, while the 14xxxxx job-cost accounts supply cost-to-date detail. MBG's real aggregate WIP is $14,480,000.00, but that portfolio total cannot determine revenue by itself. Revenue recognition is performed by contract and performance obligation using supported transaction price, eligible cost, and current estimate to complete.

Billing, cash collection, physical progress, and accounting progress often differ. A project may be underbilled even though revenue is properly recognized, or overbilled while carrying a contract liability. The accountant must identify what promise is being satisfied and choose a measure that faithfully depicts performance.

Concept — ASC 606's five-step model

  1. Identify the contract. The parties approve it, rights and payment terms are identifiable, it has commercial substance, and collection is probable under the guidance.
  2. Identify performance obligations. A promised good or service is distinct when the customer can benefit from it and the promise is separately identifiable in the contract context.
  3. Determine the transaction price. Include fixed and qualifying variable consideration, significant financing effects, noncash consideration, and consideration payable to the customer as applicable. Constrain variable amounts when a significant reversal is not sufficiently unlikely under the standard.
  4. Allocate transaction price. Allocate based on relative standalone selling prices unless a specified exception applies.
  5. Recognize revenue when or as control transfers. A performance obligation is satisfied over time if one of ASC 606's over-time criteria is met; otherwise recognition occurs at a point in time.

Construction contracts often qualify for over-time recognition because the customer controls the asset as it is created or because the work creates an asset with no alternative use and the contractor has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date. “Construction is always percentage-of-completion” is not a valid rule. Analyze the contract facts and enforceable rights.

Cost-to-cost as an input measure

When eligible costs faithfully depict performance, compute:

Progress = eligible cost incurred to date ÷ current estimated total eligible cost

Cumulative revenue = transaction price × progress

Current-period revenue = cumulative required revenue − prior-period recognized revenue

Exclude costs that distort performance when required, such as abnormal waste or certain significant uninstalled materials. Update the estimate to complete using approved scope, committed costs, productivity, procurement, and known risks. A cumulative catch-up adjustment records the amount required by the new estimate in the current period; it does not retroactively rewrite previously issued statements.

Expense recognition follows the model for the related cost. Costs that qualify for capitalization are recognized as assets and later expensed as control transfers or the asset is consumed. Other costs are expensed when incurred. Matching is useful as a consequence of asset and liability recognition, but it is not permission to defer an expense without an asset.

Worked example — from contract to current-period profit

The following job amounts are illustrative because the verified source identifies the real Global Status Report and portfolio WIP but does not provide a publishable contract-level row. Assume a single performance obligation qualifies for over-time recognition. Contract price is $3,000,000; estimated total eligible cost is $2,400,000; cost to date is $960,000; billings to date are $1,050,000; prior-period revenue is $900,000; and prior-period cost was $720,000.

MeasureCalculationAmount
Progress$960,000 ÷ $2,400,00040%
Cumulative revenue$3,000,000 × 40%$1,200,000
Cumulative profit$1,200,000 − $960,000$240,000
Current revenue$1,200,000 − $900,000$300,000
Current cost$960,000 − $720,000$240,000
Current profit$300,000 − $240,000$60,000
Contract position$1,200,000 − $1,050,000$150,000 contract asset

The job is underbilled by $150,000 because performance exceeds billings. That is a timing position, not extra revenue. If billings were $1,350,000 instead, the $150,000 excess would generally be a contract liability.

Now assume estimated total cost rises to an illustrative $2,700,000. Revised progress is $960,000 ÷ $2,700,000 = 35.56%. Cumulative revenue becomes approximately $1,066,667. Compared with $900,000 previously recognized, current revenue would be about $166,667, not $300,000. The estimate change reduces cumulative profit and produces gross-profit fade.

Variable consideration and modifications

Suppose the contract includes an illustrative $100,000 completion bonus. Estimate variable consideration using expected value or most likely amount, whichever better predicts the consideration, then apply the constraint. Do not include the full bonus solely because the project manager expects success. Consider susceptibility to factors outside control, length of uncertainty, experience with similar contracts, and the range of possible outcomes.

A modification is a separate contract when it adds distinct goods or services at a price reflecting standalone selling prices. Otherwise treatment depends on whether remaining goods are distinct from those already transferred. A modification of a single partially satisfied construction obligation commonly results in a cumulative catch-up because the existing obligation's transaction price and measure of progress change.

Close controls

  1. Tie the contract price to executed agreements and approved change orders.
  2. Confirm over-time criteria and enforceable rights with the actual contract and jurisdictional facts.
  3. Reconcile cost to exact JCS job detail and the GL.
  4. Challenge estimate to complete with operations and procurement evidence.
  5. Compare Global Status Report physical progress with cost-based progress and explain divergence.
  6. Subtract prior cumulative recognition to avoid double counting.
  7. Reconcile billings separately and classify the contract position.
  8. Review loss jobs, fade, abnormal cost, uninstalled materials, and reversals.

Do not let a spreadsheet formula substitute for judgment. A mathematically correct percentage can be materially wrong if its numerator contains another entity's costs or its denominator omits a committed subcontract.

Entries and expense recognition

Assume the illustrative job requires $300,000 of current-period revenue and $240,000 of current-period construction cost. A conceptual system records revenue and the related contract position separately from billings, while relieving or expensing eligible cost according to the entity's accounting design. The exact accounts vary, but the schedule must produce current profit of $60,000 and must not recognize the cumulative $1,200,000 a second time.

Billing $200,000 during the period debits accounts receivable and credits the billing or contract-position account; collecting $170,000 debits cash and credits receivables. Neither entry independently proves revenue. At close, cumulative recognized revenue, cumulative cost, billings, receivables, and collections must form a coherent bridge. A $30,000 increase in receivables from these illustrative billing and collection amounts is not automatically a $30,000 increase in profit.

Contract costs also require separate analysis. Incremental costs of obtaining a contract and certain fulfillment costs may qualify for capitalization under ASC 340-40 when its criteria are met; practical expedients and amortization then apply as appropriate. Costs already addressed by another standard follow that standard. General proposal effort, wasted resources, and costs that cannot be distinguished from satisfied performance are not deferred simply to protect margin.

For expected losses, consult the applicable loss guidance for the contract and recognize required losses promptly. ASC 606's revenue model does not permit an expected total loss to remain hidden in an optimistic estimate to complete.

CPA Crossover — FAR and BAR

FAR tests contract existence, distinct promises, variable consideration, allocation, over-time criteria, contract assets, contract liabilities, and journal entries. BAR emphasizes estimate reliability, margin analysis, and operational causes of fade. For both, distinguish cumulative amounts from current-period amounts and recognition from billing.

Practice and recap

Start every problem by identifying the performance obligation and timing of transfer. Only then compute progress. Label each amount as contract price, estimated cost, incurred cost, revenue, billing, collection, or profit; mixing the labels causes most errors.

Recap: ASC 606 recognizes revenue as control transfers. Cost-to-cost is one input measure, not a universal construction shortcut. Supported estimates, clean cutoff, and separate billing reconciliation turn job cost into defensible revenue.

flashcards.front: What are ASC 606's five steps?
flashcards.back: Identify the contract, identify performance obligations, determine transaction price, allocate it, and recognize revenue when or as obligations are satisfied.

flashcards.front: What is the cost-to-cost progress formula?
flashcards.back: Eligible cost incurred to date divided by current estimated total eligible cost.

flashcards.front: Does a construction contract automatically qualify for over-time revenue?
flashcards.back: No. One of ASC 606's over-time criteria must be met based on the contract facts and enforceable rights.

flashcards.front: How is current-period revenue derived from a cumulative calculation?
flashcards.back: Required cumulative revenue minus revenue recognized through the prior period.

flashcards.front: What is a contract asset in this context?
flashcards.back: A conditional right arising when recognized performance exceeds billings, subject to the contract facts.

flashcards.front: What is gross-profit fade?
flashcards.back: A decline in estimated cumulative job margin, often caused by higher expected cost or lower transaction price.

flashcards.front: How is variable consideration estimated?
flashcards.back: Use expected value or most likely amount, then apply the constraint to limit significant reversal risk.

flashcards.front: Why compare physical progress with cost-to-cost progress?
flashcards.back: A divergence can reveal distorted costs, uninstalled materials, omitted commitments, or weak estimates.

questions.q: Illustrative cost to date is $960,000 and estimated total cost is $2,400,000. Progress is:
At 40% progress on an illustrative $3,000,000 transaction price, cumulative revenue is:
Cumulative revenue is $1,200,000 and prior revenue was $900,000. Current revenue is:
Earned revenue is $1,200,000 and billings are $1,050,000. The illustrative position is:
questions.explain: Performance exceeds billings by $150,000, producing an underbilled contract-asset position.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
questions.explain: ASC 606 recognizes revenue when or as the performance obligation is satisfied.

questions.q: A bonus is possible but highly susceptible to unresolved factors outside the contractor's control. What is required?
questions.explain: Variable consideration is limited when inclusion could cause a significant future reversal.

questions.q: Estimated total cost increases while cost to date and price remain unchanged. What generally happens to cost-to-cost progress?
questions.explain: A larger denominator reduces percentage complete and may create a cumulative catch-up reduction.

weeks.title: Disclosures, Intercompany Reciprocity & Integrated Reporting (CMA P1-A · feeds FAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — equal balances can still require disclosure and elimination

Real reciprocal pairs: MBG account 89010 and Riverton account 89011 each carried $850,000.00 and netted to $0 in the completed intercompany reconciliation. MBG note receivable 89012 and Riverton note payable 89013 each carried $12,000.00 at that checkpoint. A later toolkit run detected a fictionalized $400.00 drift in the note pair, proving that yesterday's tie is not today's evidence.

Separate-entity statements report the receivable, payable, note, interest, and relevant related-party disclosures. Consolidated statements eliminate reciprocal balances and transactions because the group cannot owe itself. Elimination does not erase legal obligations from the subsidiaries' books, and it does not justify combining source ledgers.

Concept — notes make recognition understandable

Financial statements summarize; disclosures explain. Notes describe significant accounting policies, judgments, estimates, commitments, contingencies, related parties, debt terms, concentration risks, subsequent events, and disaggregated information required by the applicable framework. Good disclosure is entity-specific and material. Boilerplate that lists every possible risk can obscure the risks that actually matter.

Recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure are related but distinct. A properly recognized note receivable may still need disclosure of related-party terms, maturity, interest, collateral, collectibility, and noncash activity. A contingency not recognized may still require disclosure. Conversely, disclosure does not cure a recognition error.

Materiality considers whether omission or misstatement could reasonably influence users, based on magnitude and nature. A small related-party item can be material by nature. Aggregation should preserve useful differences; disaggregation should not bury users in immaterial detail.

Intercompany accounting from separate books to consolidation

Reciprocal accounts must agree in amount, currency, period, and counterparty before elimination. MBG 89010 is reciprocal with Riverton 89011. MBG 89012 is reciprocal with Riverton 89013. The Master Brain establishes that MBG and MF source numbers govern their intercompany positions and subsidiaries conform after investigation. Trade AP account 211 is not automatically intercompany and does not eliminate merely because entities share ownership.

Assume the fictionalized $850,000.00 pair is a payable on MBG and receivable on Riverton. A conceptual consolidation-only elimination is:

Consolidation entryDebitCredit
Intercompany payable — MBG 89010$850,000.00—
Intercompany receivable — Riverton 89011—$850,000.00

The exact normal balance and entry direction must follow the actual TB; the reciprocal amount and pair are real, while this debit/credit orientation is a conceptual illustration. The entry exists only in the consolidation layer. Posting it into MBG or Riverton would destroy each entity's legal ledger.

For the fictionalized $12,000.00 note pair, eliminate the reciprocal note balances on consolidation. Also eliminate intercompany interest income and expense and evaluate accrued interest, if any. Do not eliminate cash paid to an external bank, third-party AP, or unrelated revenue.

Reconcile before eliminating

A zero consolidated net can conceal errors if unsupported differences are forced into an elimination. Build a matrix with entity, counterparty, exact account, balance, sign, currency, cutoff, source, and variance. Compare reciprocal amounts algebraically. Investigate timing, misclassification, one-sided entries, wrong entities, currency, and duplicate postings.

The later fictionalized $400.00 drift illustrates the control. If MBG's note receivable is $12,000.00 but Riverton's note payable becomes $10,257.47, the variance is $400.00. Do not plug the consolidation entry. Trace which book changed, whether interest or principal was posted, and whether the source-of-truth entity supports an adjustment. Only supported corrections enter entity books; elimination removes the remaining valid reciprocal amounts.

Disclosure checklist for the note

  • Relationship between MBG and Riverton and nature of the transaction.
  • Recognized receivable and payable balances by entity.
  • Principal, interest rate, maturity, collateral, and repayment terms from the executed note.
  • Interest income and expense for the period.
  • Allowance or collectibility judgments when applicable.
  • Noncash changes, defaults, waivers, and subsequent events when material.

Do not invent missing terms. If the executed note has not been inspected, state that the terms require confirmation rather than filling a disclosure with assumed rates or dates.

Integrated reporting and connectivity

Integrated reporting connects financial performance with strategy, governance, risks, resources, and value creation over time. It does not replace GAAP statements. For a construction group, useful connectivity might explain how backlog, WIP, billing position, cash forecasts, supplier capacity, safety, and surety constraints affect financial outcomes.

Measures outside the financial statements need definitions, scope, period consistency, and reconciliation where appropriate. “Backlog” can differ depending on whether it includes unsigned awards or unapproved change orders. “Percent complete” can be physical, cost-based, or billing-based. Without definitions, apparent integration creates confusion.

Entity boundaries remain critical. A group dashboard can present MBG and Riverton side by side, but it must not silently blend bank balances or margins. Consolidated measures should identify eliminations. Segment or entity information should reconcile to the group total.

Worked disclosure example

The following wording is illustrative and intentionally avoids invented contract terms: “The Company engages in financing and operating transactions with Riverton, an affiliated entity. At the reporting date, the Company's intercompany payable account 89010 was $850,000.00 and its note receivable account 89012 was $12,000.00. Reciprocal balances are eliminated in consolidated reporting. Terms, settlement activity, and collectibility are evaluated from executed agreements and current reconciliations.”

That draft must be adapted to the reporting entity, actual normal balances, executed agreements, applicable disclosure requirements, and materiality. If the later $400.00 drift remains unresolved at the reporting date, it belongs on the close exception log, not hidden inside polished prose.

Subsequent events, commitments, and concentrations

Disclosures are anchored to the reporting date but may require information learned afterward. Recognized subsequent events provide additional evidence about conditions that existed at the balance-sheet date; nonrecognized events arise afterward but may require disclosure when material. The accountant must identify the underlying condition and timing, not simply the date management learned about it.

Construction disclosures may need to address commitments under major subcontracts, guarantees, surety arrangements, litigation, credit concentrations, and dependence on lenders or key suppliers. These are not inserted automatically. Inspect agreements, legal correspondence, aging reports, and governance minutes, then apply the relevant recognition and disclosure requirements. Quantify exposure when reasonably estimable and required; otherwise describe the nature and uncertainty without false precision.

Intercompany terms can create liquidity concentrations even when consolidated balances eliminate. Riverton may legally owe MBG, and each entity's standalone liquidity depends on settlement expectations. Consolidated elimination removes the group's internal receivable and payable but does not remove operational cash needs, covenant effects on separate borrowers, or governance responsibilities.

A disclosure control matrix should assign an owner, source, cutoff, preparer, reviewer, and evidence link to each note. Roll forward prior disclosures, but require current verification. The fictionalized $400.00 drift demonstrates why copying last period's $12,000.00 reciprocal note balance without rerunning the reconciliation would be unsafe.

CPA Crossover — FAR

FAR tests related-party disclosures, subsequent events, contingencies, accounting policies, segment information, and consolidation eliminations. Expect questions that distinguish entity-book entries from worksheet-only eliminations. A consolidation entry never substitutes for correcting an error on a subsidiary's books.

Practice and recap

  1. Reconcile exact reciprocal pairs at the current cutoff.
  2. Correct supported entity-level errors before consolidation.
  3. Eliminate valid reciprocal balances and transactions only in the consolidation layer.
  4. Evaluate materiality by amount and nature.
  5. Draft disclosures from executed terms and verified balances; do not invent facts.
  6. Connect nonfinancial measures to statements with clear definitions and boundaries.

Recap: disclosure explains what recognition alone cannot. Reciprocity proves intercompany balances before elimination, while integrated reporting connects financial results to operations without weakening entity or measurement discipline.

flashcards.front: What are the real MBG 89010 and Riverton 89011 reciprocal balances?
flashcards.back: $850,000.00 each at the completed reconciliation checkpoint.

flashcards.front: What are the real MBG 89012 and Riverton 89013 note balances?
flashcards.back: $12,000.00 each at the checkpoint; a later run detected a $400.00 drift.

flashcards.front: Where are intercompany eliminations posted?
flashcards.back: In the consolidation layer, not into the separate legal-entity ledgers.

flashcards.front: Does account 211 trade AP automatically eliminate?
flashcards.back: No. It is not an intercompany account merely because entities share ownership.

flashcards.front: Can disclosure cure a recognition error?
flashcards.back: No. Recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure are separate requirements.

flashcards.front: Why can a small related-party transaction be material?
flashcards.back: Materiality depends on nature as well as magnitude.

flashcards.front: What should happen when reciprocal accounts differ?
flashcards.back: Investigate timing, classification, entity, currency, and one-sided postings; do not plug the elimination.

flashcards.front: What does integrated reporting add?
flashcards.back: Connectivity among strategy, governance, risks, resources, operations, and financial outcomes; it does not replace GAAP statements.

questions.q: MBG 89010 and Riverton 89011 each show the fictionalized $850,000.00 reciprocal balance. What occurs in consolidation?
choices: The valid reciprocal balances are eliminated
questions.explain: The group cannot owe itself, so valid reciprocal receivable/payable balances are removed in consolidation.

questions.q: Where should the elimination be recorded?
questions.explain: Separate entity books retain their legal balances; the elimination belongs to consolidated reporting.

questions.q: The note pair differs by the fictionalized $400.00 drift. What is the correct first action?
choices: Trace the source and timing of the difference
questions.explain: A difference may represent a one-sided or misclassified entry and must be reconciled before elimination.

questions.q: Which item is not automatically eliminated?
questions.explain: Third-party AP remains a group obligation and is not intercompany merely because related entities exist.

questions.q: Which statement about materiality is correct?
choices: All differences must be disclosed regardless of context
questions.explain: Qualitative nature can make a smaller item important to users.

questions.q: Executed note terms have not been inspected. A disclosure should:
choices: State only verified facts and obtain the agreement
questions.explain: Disclosure must be grounded in verified balances and executed terms, with missing facts identified for confirmation.

questions.q: What is integrated reporting's relationship to GAAP statements?
choices: It connects broader value-creation information but does not replace them
questions.explain: Integrated reporting adds connectivity among financial and operational factors while GAAP reporting remains required.

m2.title: Month 2 — Planning, Budgeting & Forecasting (CMA P1-B)
m2.description: Strategic planning, budget methodologies, forecasting, pro-forma statements — on a construction group plan.

weeks.title: Strategic Planning & Budget Concepts (CMA P1-B · feeds BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — one group, different economic engines

Real MBG context: MBG's ledger control total is $12,480,000.00, Riverton's is $16,920,000.00, MBG WIP is $14,480,000.00, and Riverton WIP is $11,360,000.00. These amounts belong to separate entities. A builder and a developer can share ownership and strategic goals while having different cash cycles, risk profiles, capital needs, and performance measures. A group plan must preserve those differences before presenting any consolidated dashboard.

Strategy answers where the organization will compete and how it will create value. Planning converts strategy into objectives, initiatives, resources, timelines, and measures. A budget is the quantified short-term expression of part of that plan—not the strategy itself.

Concept — from mission to operating action

A planning hierarchy commonly includes mission, vision, values, long-term objectives, strategies, programs, annual plans, budgets, and performance feedback. Strategic planning has a multi-year horizon and considers customers, competitors, capabilities, capital, regulation, technology, and risk. Tactical plans translate strategy for functions or entities. Operational plans specify near-term volume, staffing, procurement, scheduling, and cash actions.

Useful objectives are specific, measurable, achievable but demanding, relevant, and time-bound. Objectives should balance financial outcomes with drivers such as backlog quality, cycle time, change-order control, safety, vendor compliance, and forecasting accuracy. A target without an owner and initiative is aspiration; an initiative without a measure cannot be evaluated.

Environmental analysis

SWOT separates internal strengths and weaknesses from external opportunities and threats. PESTEL considers political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal forces. Competitive analysis examines customers, suppliers, entrants, substitutes, and rivalry. These frameworks organize judgment; they do not generate a strategy automatically.

For a construction group, external factors include rates, housing demand, labor availability, material lead times, surety capacity, insurance requirements, and permitting. Internal factors include estimating accuracy, project management, liquidity, systems, controls, and entity structure. Scenario planning asks how strategies perform under coherent alternative futures instead of assigning false certainty to one forecast.

Builder versus developer planning

A builder earns through construction execution: bid discipline, cost control, schedule, change orders, quality, and collections. A developer creates value through land, entitlements, financing, design, construction, leasing or sale, and timing. The developer may consume cash for long periods before realization; the builder may generate billings while carrying underbilling and retainage exposure.

Build entity-specific plans first. MBG and Riverton each need revenue or project assumptions, cost-to-complete, WIP, billing, cash, debt, and risk. Then construct a group view with clearly identified eliminations and shared-resource assumptions. Do not add reciprocal intercompany receivables and payables as though they were external liquidity.

The real MBG and Riverton WIP balances are scale indicators, not forecasted revenue. A plan must connect each job's contract, progress, estimate to complete, billing milestones, and cash timing. Portfolio WIP can rise because activity grows, costs arrive before closings, projects slow, or classifications are wrong; interpretation requires the job schedule.

Worked strategic scorecard

The following targets are illustrative. Suppose the group objective is to protect liquidity while completing current projects. Management selects four perspectives:

PerspectiveObjectiveIllustrative measure/target
FinancialProtect liquidityMaintain minimum $1,000,000 group available liquidity, shown by entity
Customer/projectDeliver reliablyAt least 90% milestones on schedule
Internal processImprove estimate qualityMonthly cost-to-complete updates by day 3
Learning/controlStrengthen data ownership100% key reconciliations have named preparer/reviewer

The financial measure is a lagging outcome; schedule, estimate cadence, and reconciliation ownership are leading drivers. Targets must be defined. “Available liquidity” might include unrestricted cash and committed undrawn facilities, but exclude restricted cash and uncommitted borrowing. A group total should show entity restrictions so cash trapped in one entity is not assumed available to another.

Assume illustrative unrestricted cash is $600,000 at MBG and $700,000 at Riverton, while $300,000 of Riverton cash is restricted. Simple cash totals $1,300,000, but available unrestricted cash is $1,000,000. If MBG cannot legally use Riverton's remaining $400,000, MBG's own liquidity remains $600,000. Dashboard design must not erase legal boundaries.

Budget purposes and behavioral effects

Budgets coordinate functions, allocate resources, communicate expectations, authorize activity, and provide performance benchmarks. They can also create dysfunctional behavior: budgetary slack, short-termism, spending to preserve future allocations, manipulated timing, and rejection of beneficial unbudgeted opportunities.

Participation can improve information and commitment, but excessive negotiation can embed slack. Top-down budgets support strategic alignment but may ignore operational knowledge. Effective design combines direction with evidence-based challenge and separates forecasting from target setting. A forecast should be the best current estimate; turning every forecast into a performance promise encourages bias.

Controllable performance should be evaluated at the level where managers influence outcomes. A project manager should not be penalized for group financing costs outside authority, but should be accountable for supported estimates, approvals, and cost management. Shared costs require transparent allocation and separate reporting where decisions could be distorted.

Risk, sensitivity, and contingency

Identify key assumptions and ranges rather than hiding them in formulas. For an illustrative $5,000,000 project with a planned 20% gross margin, planned cost is $4,000,000. A 5% increase in planned cost adds $200,000 and reduces expected profit from $1,000,000 to $800,000, a 16% margin. Sensitivity reveals which assumptions deserve monitoring.

Contingency plans define triggers and actions. If a draw is delayed, management may defer discretionary spend, accelerate supported billing, negotiate vendor timing, or use an approved facility. Contingency is not an undisclosed plug in project cost. Distinguish known scope, quantified risk allowance, management reserve, and liquidity buffer.

Strategy execution and review cadence

Convert each initiative into a charter with objective, scope, accountable executive, operating owner, resources, milestones, dependencies, risks, and expected financial effect. For example, improving cost-to-complete accuracy may require project-manager training, a common estimate template, committed-cost integration, and a monthly review. The budget should fund those actions rather than merely reduce the desired margin fade.

Use a strategy map to show cause and effect. Better job-data ownership may improve forecast timeliness; better forecasts may enable earlier procurement and billing decisions; those actions may improve margin and liquidity. Treat the map as a testable hypothesis. If process measures improve without financial results, investigate whether the causal logic, lag, or measure is wrong.

Review strategy at a different level from weekly operations. Monthly operating reviews address exceptions and forecasts. Quarterly strategy reviews reconsider external conditions, initiative progress, resource conflicts, and whether assumptions remain valid. Annual planning resets the longer horizon but should not be the only time strategy is discussed.

Governance prevents metric gaming. Define calculation, owner, source system, frequency, threshold, and approval for each KPI. Preserve prior values and document restatements. If an entity misses a target, separate execution failure from an invalid assumption before changing incentives or resource allocation.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR emphasizes planning models, driver relationships, scenario analysis, and evaluation of management information. Questions may require identifying inconsistent assumptions across financial statements or explaining why a consolidated KPI masks segment risk. Preserve definitions, entity boundaries, and reconciliation to financial data.

Practice and recap

  1. Define separate MBG and Riverton strategic objectives and constraints.
  2. Translate objectives into owned initiatives, measures, targets, and dates.
  3. Connect job assumptions to WIP, billings, cash, and financing.
  4. Build base, upside, and downside scenarios using coherent drivers.
  5. Consolidate only after entity plans are valid and eliminations identified.
  6. Review behavior created by targets and incentives.

Recap: strategy chooses direction; planning organizes action; budgeting quantifies resources. A useful group dashboard preserves the economics and legal boundaries of builder and developer entities while showing how their decisions interact.

flashcards.front: How does strategy differ from a budget?
flashcards.back: Strategy chooses where and how to create value; a budget quantifies near-term resources and expected results.

flashcards.front: Why plan MBG and Riverton separately first?
flashcards.back: They are distinct entities with different cash, risk, WIP, financing, and legal constraints.

flashcards.front: What does SWOT distinguish?
flashcards.back: Internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats.

flashcards.front: What is scenario planning?
flashcards.back: Testing strategy under coherent alternative futures rather than relying on one point forecast.

flashcards.front: Why separate forecasts from targets?
flashcards.back: A forecast should be unbiased best estimate; a target is an aspiration or commitment and can create bias.

flashcards.front: What are leading and lagging measures?
flashcards.back: Leading measures track drivers; lagging measures report resulting outcomes.

flashcards.front: What are the real MBG and Riverton WIP balances?
What is budgetary slack?
flashcards.back: Deliberately understating capability or overstating resource needs to make a budget easier to achieve.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes a forecast from a target?
choices: A forecast is a best estimate; a target is a desired result
questions.explain: Separating predictive estimates from desired outcomes reduces bias and clarifies accountability.

questions.q: Illustrative project price is $5,000,000 and planned cost $4,000,000. Cost rises 5%. Revised expected profit is:
Which is primarily a leading indicator of project margin?
questions.explain: Current estimate discipline drives early detection of margin changes.

questions.q: Why can group cash mislead?
choices: Entity restrictions may prevent one company from using another's cash
questions.explain: Legal, contractual, and operational restrictions can make consolidated liquidity unavailable to a specific entity.

questions.q: Which behavior is a budget risk?
choices: Creating slack to make targets easier
questions.explain: Budget-linked incentives can motivate biased estimates and resource requests.

questions.q: What should happen before a group dashboard consolidates MBG and Riverton?
choices: Validate entity plans and identify eliminations
questions.explain: Valid entity-level plans are the foundation for a meaningful consolidated view.

questions.q: Which framework examines political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal forces?
questions.explain: PESTEL organizes major external macro-environmental factors.

weeks.title: Budget Methodologies — Master, Flexible, ABB, ZBB & Project Budgets (CMA P1-B · feeds BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — a job budget must speak the same language as actual cost

Real MBG structure: job cost codes roll into WIP GL accounts 1401 labor, 1402 materials, 1403 equipment, 1404 subcontractors, and 1405 other direct cost. A project budget built by phases and cost codes is useful only if JCS actuals map to the same definitions. Comparing a broad estimate category to differently classified actuals creates a variance that cannot guide action.

Budget methodology should fit the decision. A master budget coordinates the enterprise; a flexible budget separates volume from efficiency; activity-based budgeting estimates resource demand from activities; zero-based budgeting challenges discretionary spending; and a project budget controls a unique job across its lifecycle.

Master budget architecture

The master budget integrates operating and financial budgets. The sales or contract plan drives production or project activity, which drives labor, materials, subcontract, equipment, and overhead. Those budgets feed budgeted income, cash, and balance sheets. In construction, timing assumptions for draws, billings, retainage, vendor payments, and closings make the cash budget essential.

Schedules must articulate. Ending cash in the cash budget equals budgeted balance-sheet cash. Budgeted net income rolls into retained earnings. Capital spending affects cash and long-lived assets, with depreciation affecting income. Borrowing affects cash, debt, and interest. An assumption used in one schedule cannot silently differ elsewhere.

Static and flexible budgets

A static budget is based on planned activity. It is appropriate for planning but can be unfair for performance evaluation when actual volume differs. A flexible budget recalculates expected revenue and variable cost at actual activity while holding standards constant. The difference between actual results and flexible budget isolates price, efficiency, and spending effects; the difference between flexible and static budgets reflects activity volume.

Assume an illustrative project planned 100 framing units at $2,000 variable cost per unit plus $50,000 fixed site cost. Static budget is $250,000. Actual activity is 120 units, so flexible budget is 120 × $2,000 + $50,000 = $290,000. If actual cost is $310,000, the unfavorable spending/efficiency variance versus flexible budget is $20,000. Comparing actual to static budget would show $60,000 unfavorable and incorrectly attribute $40,000 of volume-related cost to performance.

Activity-based budgeting

Activity-based budgeting (ABB) forecasts activity demand from expected output, then estimates resources required. It reverses activity-based costing: first forecast jobs, change orders, purchase orders, inspections, or mobilizations; then multiply by resource consumption and rates.

Suppose illustratively procurement support costs $150 per purchase order and inspection support costs $400 per inspection. A job forecast of 80 POs and 15 inspections requires $12,000 + $6,000 = $18,000. A labor-hour-only budget could miss the support burden of a complex job. ABB is strongest when activity drivers are measurable and causally related; it becomes costly when every minor activity receives a pool.

Zero-based and incremental budgeting

Incremental budgeting starts with the current budget or actual and adjusts it. It is efficient for stable operations but perpetuates waste and outdated assumptions. Zero-based budgeting (ZBB) organizes discretionary work into decision packages, evaluates purpose and service level, and ranks funding from zero. ZBB does not mean every contractual or production cost is literally renegotiated from nothing each month.

An illustrative administrative software budget of $120,000 could be divided into required core licenses $70,000, enhanced analytics $30,000, and optional collaboration tools $20,000. Management ranks packages against objectives and risk rather than applying a blanket 5% cut. The analysis should include switching cost, control implications, and downstream labor—not price alone.

Project budgeting and cost-code control

A construction project budget begins with scope, quantities, production assumptions, unit rates, subcontract quotes, labor plan, equipment, permits, overhead policy, contingency, and schedule. Baseline changes require approved change control. Forecast at completion is distinct from original budget:

Forecast at completion = actual cost to date + current estimate to complete

Cost variance at completion = budget at completion − forecast at completion

Assume an illustrative job budget maps $100,000 labor to 1401, $250,000 materials to 1402, $50,000 equipment to 1403, $400,000 subcontractors to 1404, and $20,000 other direct cost to 1405. Total baseline is $820,000. Actual to date is $500,000 and current estimate to complete is $360,000, so forecast at completion is $860,000 and expected cost variance is $40,000 unfavorable.

Do not “fix” the original budget to equal the forecast. Preserve baseline, approved changes, current forecast, and actual separately. Otherwise management loses the history of estimating accuracy and scope decisions.

Contingency and change control

Contingency addresses identified uncertainty within defined scope; management reserve may address broader unknowns at a higher control level. Neither is revenue or profit. Define who can release contingency and how usage is documented.

A change order can affect contract price, budget, forecast, billing, and revenue recognition. Track proposed, submitted, approved, and rejected status. Do not add unapproved value to both contract price and project budget as if collection were certain. Scenario analysis can show outcomes while accounting follows supported terms.

Variance investigation

Set thresholds using amount, percentage, trend, risk, and controllability. A small recurring variance may reveal a broken standard; a large favorable variance may reflect missing invoices. Investigation should identify quantity, rate, mix, timing, classification, scope, and estimate changes.

Reconcile cost-code actuals to exact WIP GL control accounts before interpreting variance. A miscode between 1402 and 1404 changes category performance but not total WIP. A wrong entity changes both accountability and financial reporting.

Integrate the cash and balance-sheet budgets

A project cost budget does not reveal when cash leaves. Convert labor to payroll dates, materials to purchase and payment terms, subcontracts to progress payments and retainage, and overhead to recurring schedules. Align owner billings and draws with milestone, approval, and collection lags. The resulting cash schedule identifies financing needs before they become emergencies.

Budgeted WIP is a rollforward, not a percentage of revenue by default. Beginning WIP plus capitalizable job additions minus cost transferred on closings equals ending WIP. Budgeted AP follows received-but-unpaid costs, while retainage remains a separate obligation. Debt follows the loan schedule and interest calculation. These balance-sheet schedules must reconcile to the income and cash budgets.

Responsibility reporting should use the appropriate budget. A project manager can be evaluated against a flexible project budget and supported forecast; treasury against cash and financing; procurement against price, availability, and quality; finance against integration and forecast accuracy. Avoid assigning one undifferentiated total variance to a person who cannot control its drivers.

Document approved budget transfers. Moving dollars between codes can be legitimate after scope clarification, but it must not erase a cost overrun. Show original baseline, approved transfers, revised budget, actual, commitments, estimate to complete, and forecast at completion.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR tests budget integration, flexible-budget mechanics, driver-based forecasting, and variance interpretation. It may ask which budget changes with actual activity or why a favorable result is not necessarily good. Always identify the comparison basis before calculating a variance.

Practice and recap

  1. Select methodology based on the decision and cost behavior.
  2. Map budget lines to the same cost codes and GL controls used by actuals.
  3. Preserve baseline, approved changes, forecast, and actual separately.
  4. Flex variable cost for actual activity before judging performance.
  5. Use ABB for meaningful support drivers and ZBB for discretionary packages.
  6. Investigate missing, late, and misclassified costs before celebrating favorable variances.

Recap: no budget method is universally best. The master budget coordinates, the flexible budget normalizes volume, ABB models activity, ZBB challenges need, and the project budget controls scope and cost through a stable baseline and current forecast.

flashcards.front: What is a flexible budget?
flashcards.back: A budget recalculated at actual activity using standard variable rates and expected fixed cost.

flashcards.front: What does ABB forecast first?
flashcards.back: Activity demand, then resources and costs required for those activities.

flashcards.front: What is ZBB best suited to challenge?
flashcards.back: Discretionary activities and service levels through ranked decision packages.

flashcards.front: What is forecast at completion?
flashcards.back: Actual cost to date plus current estimate to complete.

flashcards.front: Why preserve the original project baseline?
flashcards.back: It retains accountability for estimating, scope changes, and forecast evolution.

flashcards.front: What WIP GL accounts receive the five job-cost categories?
flashcards.back: 1401 labor, 1402 materials, 1403 equipment, 1404 subcontractors, 1405 other direct.

flashcards.front: Why can a favorable cost variance be suspicious?
flashcards.back: It may reflect missing invoices, cutoff errors, or incomplete activity rather than efficiency.

flashcards.front: What is the activity variance?
flashcards.back: The difference between flexible and static budgets caused by actual activity differing from planned activity.

questions.q: Illustrative variable cost is $2,000 per unit, fixed cost $50,000, and actual activity 120 units. Flexible budget is:
If actual cost is $310,000 and flexible budget $290,000, the variance is:
questions.explain: Actual exceeds flexible expectation by $20,000.

questions.q: Which method starts by forecasting purchase orders and inspections?
questions.explain: ABB uses forecast activity drivers to estimate resource needs.

questions.q: Actual to date is $500,000 and estimate to complete $360,000. Forecast at completion is:
Budget at completion is $820,000 and forecast at completion $860,000. Expected cost variance is:
questions.explain: Forecast exceeds budget by $40,000, an unfavorable cost outlook.

questions.q: What is the main weakness of incremental budgeting?
choices: It can perpetuate waste and outdated assumptions
questions.explain: Starting from prior spending can embed activities that no longer support strategy.

questions.q: Why should baseline and forecast remain separate?
choices: To preserve original commitment and show current expected outcome
questions.explain: The baseline measures approved plan; the forecast updates expected results without rewriting history.

weeks.title: Forecasting Techniques & the 13-Week Cash Forecast (CMA P1-B · feeds P2-A)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — WIP is not cash

Real MBG context: MBG carries $14,480,000.00 of WIP and Riverton $11,360,000.00. Those assets do not pay payroll tomorrow. Cash depends on billing milestones, owner draws, retainage, collections, vendor terms, debt service, and project timing. The group also identified $400,000.00 stranded across seven dormant bank accounts, showing that total cash and usable cash can differ.

A 13-week cash forecast converts project and operating events into weekly receipts, disbursements, financing needs, and minimum cash. Its short horizon supports action while extending far enough to expose draw delays, payroll cycles, tax dates, and vendor peaks.

Forecast architecture

Begin with independently reconciled opening cash by entity and bank account. Then forecast cash receipts and disbursements by week:

Ending cash = Beginning cash + receipts − disbursements + financing inflows − financing repayments

Ending cash becomes the next week's beginning cash. Compare projected ending cash with required minimum cash to calculate borrowing or surplus. Do not include WIP, underbillings, or available credit as cash receipts until a supported timing event occurs.

Receipt drivers

  • Approved billing schedule and expected invoice submission.
  • Collection lag by owner/customer and historical behavior.
  • Construction draws tied to inspections or completion milestones.
  • Retainage releases only when contractual conditions are supportable.
  • Asset sales, tax refunds, equity, or debt based on approved evidence.

Disbursement drivers

  • Payroll through PayStream ACH or MBG check—never cash labor.
  • AP aging, vendor commitments, subcontract schedules, and retainage releases.
  • Taxes, insurance, debt service, equipment, and corporate overhead.
  • Intercompany transfers shown by both entities and eliminated only in a group cash bridge.

Worked 4-week slice

The following cash amounts are illustrative. MBG begins Week 1 with $500,000 and requires minimum cash of $250,000.

WeekBeginningReceiptsDisbursementsPre-financing endingBorrowing needed
1$500,000$300,000$450,000$350,000$0
2$350,000$200,000$400,000$150,000$100,000
3$250,000$600,000$300,000$550,000$0
4$550,000$150,000$500,000$200,000$50,000

After Week 2 borrowing, ending cash is $250,000 and becomes Week 3 beginning cash. If Week 4 also borrows $50,000, cumulative facility use is $150,000 before repayments. The forecast should show capacity, interest, covenant, approval, and availability rather than assuming borrowing is automatic.

Suppose Week 3's $600,000 receipt depends on a draw inspection that slips one week. Week 3 pre-financing ending becomes negative $50,000: $250,000 + $0 − $300,000. To preserve minimum cash, Week 3 requires $300,000 borrowing, not $0. Week 4 then receives the delayed $600,000 plus its planned $150,000, changing repayment capacity. Timing sensitivity matters more than quarterly totals.

Forecasting methods

Naive and moving-average methods extrapolate recent observations and work for stable recurring costs. A three-period moving average smooths noise but lags turning points. Exponential smoothing weights recent actuals more heavily; a higher smoothing constant reacts faster but increases volatility.

Regression estimates relationships such as labor hours driven by units installed. The equation Y = a + bX separates intercept and driver effect. Correlation does not prove causation; validate economic logic, residuals, stability, outliers, and relevant range.

Expected value probability-weights discrete outcomes. If an illustrative draw has 70% probability of $500,000 this week and 30% probability of $0, expected value is $350,000. For liquidity management, showing both scenarios may be safer than placing $350,000 in the cash column because no actual outcome pays $350,000.

Learning curves model declining cumulative average time as experience doubles. They fit repetitive work, not every custom construction task. Time-series decomposition separates trend, seasonality, cyclical, and irregular components; it requires enough consistent history.

Link WIP and draws without equating them

For each active job, forecast cost outflow, eligible progress, billing or draw trigger, submission date, approval lag, retainage, and collection date. Compare percentage complete, percentage billed, and percentage drawn. Divergence is a diagnostic, not automatically an error.

An underbilled job may signal an upcoming receipt opportunity or an unapproved/collectibility problem. An overbilled job may support current cash but creates future performance without equivalent billing. Cost-to-complete increases can raise future cash need while reducing margin. Update both the WIP forecast and cash forecast from the same operational facts.

Use the real WIP balances as reconciliation anchors, not as forecast receipts. MBG and Riverton forecasts remain separate because bank and funding access are entity-specific. A group view shows intercompany transfers twice at entity level—outflow and inflow—then eliminates them from group net cash movement.

Rolling forecast governance

Every week, replace forecast with actual, explain variance, and add a new week so the horizon remains 13 weeks. Lock prior versions. Track forecast accuracy by category and horizon: Week 1 should generally be more accurate than Week 13. Separate timing variance from amount variance.

Assign owners: project teams own milestone evidence; AP owns payment schedules; payroll owns payroll dates; treasury owns bank and financing; finance integrates and challenges. Maintain a source and confidence rating for material receipts. Do not let a favorable plug restore minimum cash.

Base, downside, and severe-but-plausible scenarios should specify triggers and actions. A downside case can delay major draws, accelerate material purchases, or reduce available credit. Avoid double-counting correlated risks.

Accuracy measurement and backtesting

Forecast error should be measured consistently. For a cash category, error can be actual minus forecast; absolute error removes favorable/unfavorable direction; percentage error scales for size but becomes unstable near zero. Mean absolute error is easy to explain, while mean absolute percentage error can overemphasize small denominators. Bias is the signed average error and reveals systematic optimism or conservatism.

Assume illustrative weekly receipts were forecast at $400,000, $500,000, and $300,000, while actuals were $350,000, $650,000, and $250,000. Signed errors actual minus forecast are negative $50,000, positive $150,000, and negative $50,000. Mean signed error is positive $16,666.67, while mean absolute error is $83,333.33. The positive bias is not proof of accuracy; large offsetting errors can produce a small average.

Backtesting asks whether assumptions performed as expected and why. Classify misses as timing, amount, scope, source-data, or judgment. Repeated owner-payment delays should change the collection-lag assumption. A one-time storm may remain a scenario risk rather than a new base trend. Record forecast changes prospectively; do not rewrite archived versions.

Use confidence tiers for receipts: committed and confirmed, probable with evidence, and scenario-only. Apply stronger challenge to large, late-horizon, or externally dependent receipts. Forecast governance should prohibit using unsupported intercompany transfers or new debt merely to eliminate a projected deficit.

Regression discipline

Before using a regression, plot the data, inspect sample size and outliers, test whether the relationship makes operational sense, and avoid extrapolating outside the observed range. Structural changes—new labor process, entity, or pricing—can make historical coefficients obsolete. Forecasting is a controlled learning process, not permanent trust in one equation.

CMA Part 2 Crossover — Financial Statement Analysis
