weeks.title: Common-Size, Trend & Segment Analysis — Comparing MBG and Riverton Fairly (CMA P2-A · feeds BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — you cannot compare a $12.5M entity to a $16.9M entity by dollars

Real MBG facts: the MBG GL totals $12,480,000.00 and Riverton totals $16,920,000.00, and a standing rule is that the two entities are never combined on one statement — each is reported as its own segment. So how do you tell which entity is structurally healthier when one is a third larger? You normalize. Common-size analysis restates every line as a percentage, removing the size effect so structure and trend become comparable across entities and across years.

Vertical (common-size) analysis

Common-size the income statement by dividing every line by revenue, and the balance sheet by dividing every line by total assets. Using week 2's illustrative MBG statements:

Common-size income statement (÷ revenue $24,000,000)

Revenue 100.0%; cost of revenue 86.0%; gross profit 14.0%; general & administrative 7.5%; operating income 6.5%; interest 1.08%; pretax income 5.42%; income tax 1.30%; net income 4.12%. Now a margin problem is visible regardless of revenue size — a contractor whose cost of revenue runs 90% has a 10% gross margin no matter how big the top line is.

Common-size balance sheet (÷ total assets $12,000,000)

Current assets 50.0%; net property & equipment 41.7%; other 8.3%; current liabilities 25.0%; long-term debt & other 40.0%; total liabilities 65.0%; equity 35.0%. The 65% liability share is the same story as week 1's debt-to-assets of 0.65 — common-size and ratios are two views of the same structure.

Horizontal (trend) analysis

Horizontal analysis compares the same line across periods. Assume an illustrative prior year with revenue $21,000,000 and net income $760,000.

Revenue growth = ($24,000,000 − $21,000,000) ÷ $21,000,000 = 14.3%. Expressed as a trend index with the prior year = 100, current revenue indexes to ($24,000,000 ÷ $21,000,000) × 100 = 114.3.

Net income growth = ($988,000 − $760,000) ÷ $760,000 = 30.0%. Net income grew far faster than revenue (30.0% vs 14.3%), which means the net margin expanded — from $760,000 ÷ $21,000,000 = 3.62% last year to 4.12% this year. Trend plus common-size together tell you not just that profit rose, but that it rose because of margin, not just volume.

Segment comparison — MBG vs Riverton

Because the entities are reported separately (a real consolidation rule — never combine MBG and Riverton), common-size is the honest way to compare them. Suppose Riverton's common-size cost of revenue is 88.0% versus MBG's 86.0%. Riverton is the larger entity by GL dollars ($14.03M vs $10.60M) yet converts a smaller share of each revenue dollar into gross profit. Size hid that; common-size reveals it. The same approach compares either entity to industry benchmarks, since published construction benchmarks are expressed as percentages.

Segment reporting discipline matters: combining the two would overstate scale and mask that the structural margin difference lives in one entity. The intercompany balances between them (covered next week) must be eliminated before any consolidated view — but for performance comparison, you keep them separate and common-size each.

Market ratios and the private-company limit

Market-based ratios extend analysis to share value: earnings per share = net income ÷ weighted-average shares; price/earnings = market price per share ÷ EPS; dividend yield = dividends per share ÷ market price. These require a traded price. MBG is privately held, so there is no market price and P/E cannot be computed directly. Analysts instead apply comparable public-company multiples or precedent-transaction multiples to MBG's earnings to estimate value. Recognizing this limit is itself an exam point: do not report a market ratio for an entity that has no market price.

Combining the two lenses — and the benchmarks that matter

Vertical and horizontal analysis are most powerful together. A common-size statement tells you the structure in one period; a trend index tells you the direction; reading both at once isolates the cause of a change. Suppose MBG's cost of revenue rose from 84.0% to 86.0% of revenue (vertical) while revenue grew 14.3% (horizontal). The combined read is unambiguous: the business got bigger but less efficient per dollar — volume up, margin compressed — which is a very different story from a contractor whose margin held as it grew. On the income statement, the gross-profit line is the one to watch in construction; on the balance sheet, the current-liability and equity percentages reveal the leverage structure that month one's debt-to-assets ratio measured directly.

Choosing benchmarks. A common-size or trend figure is meaningless in isolation; it needs a comparator. The three standard references are the entity's own history (is the structure drifting?), close peers, and published industry data — for construction, sources such as surety and contractor financial surveys that report median percentages by revenue band. Because those benchmarks are expressed as percentages, common-size is the only way to line MBG, Riverton, and an industry median up on the same axis. The size gap that made the raw GL totals ($12.5M vs $16.9M) incomparable disappears once every line is a share of its own base.

Pitfalls in common-size and trend work

Several traps recur. First, a small or volatile base distorts a trend index — a line that grows from $2,000 to $4,000 shows a 100% jump that means little in dollars. Second, changing the denominator mid-comparison (revenue redefined, a segment reclassified) silently breaks the trend, the same reprocessing risk the CMA program flagged when a crosswalk version changed. Third, reading a percentage shift without the dollar context: a 1-point rise in cost of revenue on $24,000,000 of revenue is $240,000 of lost gross profit — material to a contractor's thin margin even though "one point" sounds trivial. Always carry the percentage back to dollars before concluding.

What common-size cannot tell you

Normalizing is powerful but it discards one thing on purpose: absolute scale. Two contractors can show nearly identical common-size statements while one is ten times the size of the other — with very different access to bonding, financing, skilled crews, and economies of scale. Percentages can also mask a shrinking business: a firm in decline may hold a stable common-size profile while its dollars steadily erode, which is exactly why common-size is always paired with horizontal dollar-and-index analysis. And a percentage built on a tiny or negative base — near-zero equity, a loss year — can be mathematically valid yet analytically meaningless. Use common-size to compare structure across entities and time; never let it stand in for the absolute dollars, the trend, and the business context behind them.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR pairs common-size and horizontal analysis with interpretation: identify which line drove a margin change, compute a trend index, and read a common-size statement against a benchmark. Expect a question where revenue and net income grow at different rates and you must conclude whether margins expanded or contracted. The segment-comparison logic — normalize before comparing entities of different size — is squarely BAR territory.

Practice and recap

  1. Common-size the income statement (÷ revenue) and balance sheet (÷ total assets).
  2. Compute horizontal growth rates and a trend index against a base year.
  3. Infer margin expansion or contraction by comparing revenue growth to net-income growth.
  4. Use common-size to compare MBG and Riverton — never by combining them.
  5. Know why a private company has no P/E and what is used instead.

Recap: common-size removes size so structure is comparable; trend analysis shows direction; together they reveal that MBG's net income grew 30.0% on 14.3% revenue growth because the margin expanded. Different-sized entities like MBG and Riverton compare only after normalizing.

weeks.title: Special Issues — Intercompany Eliminations, FX & Fair Value (CMA P2-A · feeds FAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — two real balances that must vanish on consolidation

Real MBG facts: the intercompany payable on MBG account 89010 is reciprocal with Riverton's intercompany receivable 89011, and MBG's note receivable 89012 is reciprocal with Riverton's note payable 89013. Both reciprocal pairs tie at their checkpoints — MBG 89010 and Riverton 89011 each at $850,000.00, and MBG 89012 and Riverton 89013 each at $12,000.00 — equal and opposite, so they eliminate on consolidation. (A later run found a real $400.00 drift on the note pair, a live example of the very control this week is about.) That is not an accident — it is the control that lets the balances be eliminated in any consolidated view. This week covers the analysis issues that sit outside the standard ratios: intercompany eliminations, foreign currency, and fair value.

Intercompany eliminations

When related entities transact, each side records its half: MBG owes Riverton, so MBG carries a payable (89010) and Riverton carries the matching receivable (89011). If you simply added the two entities together, consolidated assets and liabilities would both be overstated by the same intercompany amount — a company cannot owe or be owed by itself. Consolidation therefore eliminates reciprocal intercompany receivables and payables, notes, and any intercompany revenue/expense or unrealized profit.

The control discipline: the reciprocal accounts must be equal and opposite before elimination. MBG 89010 must equal Riverton 89011; MBG note receivable 89012 must equal Riverton note payable 89013. A non-zero net would flag a missing entry, a timing cutoff, or a posting error — you investigate the difference rather than plug it. The ICP pair nets to zero, but the note pair's $400.00 drift is exactly such a flag: it must be investigated, not plugged. Note that this is distinct from performance comparison (week 3), where the entities stay separate; elimination applies only to the consolidated view.

This is also a useful sense of off-balance-sheet: the intercompany note that is a real asset on MBG's own books does not appear at all on the consolidated balance sheet because it nets against Riverton's payable.

Foreign currency (ASC 830)

The functional currency is the currency of the primary economic environment in which an entity operates; the reporting currency is the one the financial statements are presented in. Three situations the exam separates:

  • Foreign-currency transaction — MBG buys equipment priced in euros and settles later. The exchange-rate change between purchase and settlement creates a transaction gain or loss recognized in net income.
  • Translation — a foreign subsidiary keeps books in its functional currency and is translated to the reporting currency using the current-rate method. The resulting translation adjustment goes to other comprehensive income (the cumulative translation adjustment), not net income.
  • Remeasurement — books kept in a currency other than the functional currency are remeasured into the functional currency, and those gains/losses do hit net income.

The exam trap is the destination: transaction and remeasurement effects flow through income; translation under the current-rate method parks in OCI as CTA until the foreign operation is sold.

Fair value (ASC 820)

Fair value is an exit price in an orderly transaction between market participants. The measurement hierarchy ranks the inputs, not the assets:

  • Level 1 — quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities (most reliable).
  • Level 2 — observable inputs other than Level 1: quoted prices for similar items, quoted prices in inactive markets, or other observable data.
  • Level 3 — unobservable inputs, such as management's own discounted-cash-flow assumptions (least reliable, most disclosure).

A contractor estimating the fair value of a custom, non-traded asset by its own cash-flow model is using Level 3 inputs and must disclose the assumptions and sensitivity.

Off-balance-sheet items and disclosure

Historically, operating leases, certain guarantees, and special-purpose entities kept obligations off the balance sheet. Under ASC 842, a lessee now recognizes a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for operating leases, bringing most lease obligations on-balance-sheet. Items that remain off the face of the statements but affect risk — performance and payment bonds, surety commitments, retainage obligations, and contract backlog — are addressed through disclosure. An analyst adjusts leverage and coverage for material off-balance-sheet commitments before concluding on solvency.

A worked foreign-currency transaction

Walk the mechanics that the destination rule sits on top of. Suppose MBG orders specialized equipment from a European supplier for €100,000 when the spot rate is €1 = $1.08. At the order/recognition date it records the asset and payable at $108,000 (€100,000 × 1.08). Sixty days later, at settlement, the rate has moved to €1 = $1.12, so MBG must pay $112,000 to buy the euros. The $4,000 difference is a foreign-currency transaction loss recognized in net income — the dollar weakened against the euro, so settling the same €100,000 obligation cost more dollars, and the loss is real cash. Had the rate fallen to $1.05, MBG would record a $3,000 transaction gain. The asset's recorded cost stays $108,000 either way; only the settlement of the monetary liability produces the income-statement effect. This is the income-versus-OCI line drawn precisely: a settled transaction hits earnings, while translating a foreign subsidiary under the current-rate method would instead park the adjustment in OCI.

Fair-value disclosure and analyst adjustments

Beyond classifying inputs as Level 1, 2, or 3, FAR-style reporting requires disclosure proportional to subjectivity: Level 3 measurements demand the valuation technique, the significant unobservable inputs, and often a sensitivity analysis showing how the estimate moves with the assumptions. The less observable the input, the more an informed reader should discount management's number — a recurring theme from the CMA data-integrity scars.

For off-balance-sheet items, a careful analyst re-leverages the statements before judging solvency: capitalize the present value of material operating commitments and guarantees, add them to debt, and recompute debt-to-equity and times-interest-earned on the adjusted figures. A contractor that looks comfortably leveraged on its face statements can look very different once surety obligations, large purchase commitments, and guarantees are pulled into view. Reading the face of the statements is necessary; reading the notes is where the real exposure — and the real exam points — live.

Where each effect lands — a quick map

Because the destination is the most-tested point, hold this map for the items in this lesson: a settled foreign-currency transaction and a remeasurement into the functional currency both hit net income; a current-rate translation of a foreign operation goes to OCI as the cumulative translation adjustment. Fair value is ranked by input observability — Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable — with required disclosure rising as observability falls. Intercompany receivables, payables, and notes eliminate entirely on consolidation, so they never inflate the consolidated balance sheet. And under ASC 842, the operating lease that once sat off-balance-sheet now appears on it as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. Fix these destinations in memory and most FAR foreign-currency, fair-value, and lease questions resolve on sight; the arithmetic is usually the easy part.

CPA Crossover — FAR

FAR tests these cold: eliminate intercompany balances and unrealized profit in consolidation, place a foreign-currency effect in income versus OCI, and classify a fair-value input as Level 1, 2, or 3. The reciprocal-account control here (89010↔89011, 89012↔89013 must be equal before elimination) is the same logic FAR uses for consolidation worksheets, and ASC 830/820/842 are core FAR standards.

Practice and recap

  1. Eliminate reciprocal intercompany receivables/payables and notes in the consolidated view; verify they are equal before elimination.
  2. Route a foreign-currency transaction or remeasurement gain to income; route a current-rate translation adjustment to OCI (CTA).
  3. Classify a fair-value input as Level 1, 2, or 3 by its observability.
  4. Recognize operating leases on-balance-sheet under ASC 842 and adjust for remaining off-balance-sheet commitments.

Recap: MBG's reciprocal intercompany pairs are equal and opposite (89010/89011 at $850,000.00; 89012/89013 at $12,000.00) so they eliminate cleanly on consolidation — and the note pair's $400.00 drift shows the control catching a real difference. Foreign-currency effects split between income and OCI by type, fair value is ranked by input observability, and most lease obligations now sit on the balance sheet.

weeks.title: Risk, Return, CAPM & the Cost of Capital (WACC) (CMA P2-B · feeds BAR/REG)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — what return must a new MBG job clear?

Real MBG fact: the vehicle and equipment loan portfolio totals $310,000.00 and carries interest that is real, deductible cash cost. Before MBG commits capital to a new spec build or a piece of equipment, it needs a hurdle rate — the minimum return that compensates everyone who funded the company. That hurdle is the weighted-average cost of capital (WACC), and it is built from the cost of debt and the cost of equity. This week derives both and assembles the hurdle rate.

Risk and return — first principles

Investors require higher expected return for higher risk. Total risk splits into systematic risk (market-wide, undiversifiable — interest rates, recessions) and unsystematic risk (firm-specific — a single job loss, a key-person event). Diversification removes unsystematic risk, so the market only pays a premium for systematic risk. Beta measures systematic risk: a beta of 1.0 moves with the market, above 1.0 is more volatile, below 1.0 is less.

Cost of equity — CAPM

The capital asset pricing model prices the return equity holders require:

Cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta × market risk premium.

Using illustrative market inputs appropriate to a closely held contractor: risk-free rate 4.0%, beta 1.25, market risk premium 6.0%. Cost of equity = 4.0% + 1.25 × 6.0% = 4.0% + 7.5% = 11.5%. The 1.25 beta says MBG's equity is judged 25% more cyclically sensitive than the market — reasonable for construction, which amplifies the economic cycle.

Cost of debt — and why it is after-tax

The relevant cost of debt is the after-tax rate, because interest is tax-deductible. With an illustrative pre-tax cost of debt of 8.0% on the fictionalized $310,000.00 portfolio and a 24% tax rate:

After-tax cost of debt = pre-tax rate × (1 − tax rate) = 8.0% × (1 − 0.24) = 8.0% × 0.76 = 6.08%. The tax shield is what makes debt cheaper than equity on a stated-rate basis — but more debt also raises financial risk, which feeds back into a higher beta and cost of equity.

Assembling WACC

WACC weights each source by its share of total capital:

WACC = (weight of debt × after-tax cost of debt) + (weight of equity × cost of equity).

Using an illustrative target capital structure of 40% debt and 60% equity:

WACC = (0.40 × 6.08%) + (0.60 × 11.5%) = 2.432% + 6.9% = 9.33%.

So MBG should require at least about 9.33% on projects of average risk. A spec home or equipment purchase that cannot clear this rate destroys value even if it shows accounting profit. Higher-risk projects deserve a higher project-specific rate; lower-risk ones, a lower rate. Using one firm-wide WACC for every project is a common but dangerous shortcut.

Marginal cost and weights that matter

Capital budgeting uses the marginal cost of capital — the cost of the next dollar raised — and target (often market-value) weights, not historical book weights, because new financing is what funds new projects. As a firm exhausts cheaper sources, the marginal cost of capital steps up. For a private contractor without a market price, the equity weight and beta are estimated from comparable public companies (the same private-company limit seen in week 3 of month 7).

Completing the capital structure — preferred stock and flotation

A full WACC includes every financing source. Cost of preferred stock = preferred dividend ÷ net issuance price; because preferred dividends are not tax-deductible, there is no tax adjustment. If MBG issued preferred paying a $6 dividend at a $80 net price, the cost would be $6 ÷ $80 = 7.5%, slotted into WACC at its weight. Flotation costs — the fees of issuing new securities — raise the effective cost of new external capital; they are best handled as an addition to the project's initial outlay rather than baked into a higher discount rate, but the exam also tests adjusting the cost of new equity for flotation by dividing the dividend by the net (after-flotation) price.

Cost of debt is a yield, not a coupon. A recurring error is using a bond's stated coupon as the cost of debt. The relevant pre-tax cost is the current market yield to maturity on debt of comparable risk — what MBG would pay to borrow today — then multiplied by (1 − tax rate). For the fictionalized $310,000.00 portfolio, the cost of debt for new-project analysis is the rate on new equipment financing now, not the historical rate on loans already on the books.

Project- and division-specific rates

Using a single firm-wide WACC for every project quietly subsidizes risky projects and penalizes safe ones. For a project whose risk differs from the firm's average, the technique is a pure-play beta: take comparable public companies in that line of work, unlever their betas to strip out their financing, relever at MBG's target structure, run CAPM, and rebuild a project-specific WACC. A speculative land development deserves a higher hurdle than a routine equipment replacement, and forcing both through one 9.33% rate misallocates capital.

A sensitivity and the common traps

WACC is sensitive to the inputs. Hold cost of equity 11.5% and after-tax cost of debt 6.08% but shift the structure from 40/60 debt/equity to 50/50: WACC = (0.50 × 6.08%) + (0.50 × 11.5%) = 3.04% + 5.75% = 8.79%. More debt lowers the stated WACC because debt is cheaper — but only up to the point where the added financial risk raises both the cost of equity (a higher beta) and the cost of debt, which is the optimal-capital-structure tension of next week. Three traps to avoid: using book weights instead of target/market weights, forgetting the tax shield on debt, and applying the firm WACC to an off-risk project. Each one produces a hurdle rate that accepts value-destroying work or rejects value-creating work.

WACC is a living number

A firm's WACC is not set once. It moves as interest rates change, as leverage drifts from target, as the firm's risk profile shifts, and as the market's required equity premium rises or falls. Using a stale WACC — last year's 9.33% after rates have climbed a point — systematically overvalues new projects by discounting their cash flows too lightly. Good practice re-estimates the rate periodically and whenever the capital structure or rate environment changes materially, and states the date and assumptions behind it. The discount rate is the single most leveraged assumption in any valuation: a one-point error in WACC can swing a long-lived project's net present value more than a sizable error in any single year's cash-flow forecast, which is why the rate deserves as much scrutiny as the projections it discounts.

CPA Crossover — BAR / REG

BAR tests CAPM, after-tax cost of debt, and WACC computation, plus the reasoning that a project must clear the risk-adjusted hurdle. REG reinforces why interest's deductibility drives the after-tax cost of debt. Expect a question that gives the wrong sign on the tax adjustment (using pre-tax debt in WACC) as a distractor.

Practice and recap

  1. Separate systematic from unsystematic risk; know beta measures the former.
  2. Compute cost of equity with CAPM.
  3. Convert pre-tax to after-tax cost of debt with (1 − tax rate).
  4. Weight the sources to get WACC and use it as the project hurdle.

Recap: with cost of equity 11.5%, after-tax cost of debt 6.08%, and a 40/60 structure, MBG's WACC is about 9.33%. That is the floor a new job's return must clear to create value.

weeks.title: Long-Term Financing, Leverage & Bonding Capacity (CMA P2-B · feeds BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — for a contractor, financing capacity is bonding capacity

A contractor's growth is capped less by its bank line than by its surety bonding capacity, and bonding is driven by working capital and equity. MBG's illustrative working capital from month 7 was $3,000,000 and equity $4,200,000. This week covers how firms raise long-term capital, the trade-offs between debt and equity, how financial leverage magnifies returns and risk, and the construction-specific limit that bonding imposes.

Debt versus equity

Debt is cheaper (interest is deductible — week 1), does not dilute ownership, and imposes discipline, but it adds fixed obligations, covenants, and bankruptcy risk. Equity carries no repayment obligation and absorbs downturns, but it is more expensive, dilutes control, and shares upside. The financing decision balances cost, control, flexibility, and risk. A firm with volatile cash flows — like a contractor exposed to the cycle — generally supports less debt than a stable utility.

Long-term sources include term loans, equipment financing (the fictionalized $310,000.00 portfolio), bonds, mezzanine debt, retained earnings, and outside equity. Retained earnings are not free — their opportunity cost is the cost of equity from week 1.

Financial leverage

Financial leverage uses fixed-cost financing to magnify returns to equity. The degree of financial leverage (DFL) measures the magnification:

DFL = EBIT ÷ (EBIT − interest).

Using month 7's figures, EBIT $1,560,000 and interest $260,000: DFL = $1,560,000 ÷ ($1,560,000 − $260,000) = $1,560,000 ÷ $1,300,000 = 1.2. A 1% change in EBIT produces a 1.2% change in net income (and EPS). Leverage cuts both ways: it amplifies gains when EBIT rises and losses when it falls. This is the same equity multiplier effect seen in DuPont — more leverage raises ROE but also raises the chance of distress.

Bonding capacity — the construction constraint

Sureties extend bonding based on working capital and equity, applying a multiplier. Using illustrative but conventional multipliers — aggregate program around 10× working capital and a single-job limit around 5× working capital — MBG's $3,000,000 working capital supports roughly a $30,000,000 aggregate bonding program and a $15,000,000 single-job limit. Anything that reduces working capital (over-distribution, slow retainage collection, a loss job) directly shrinks the work MBG can bond. This is why the liquidity and leverage ratios from month 7 are not academic — they set the ceiling on revenue. Retaining earnings to build working capital is often the highest-return financing decision a contractor makes.

Raising capital and EPS effects

When choosing between a debt issue and an equity issue, analysts compare the effect on EPS and on risk. Debt financing keeps shares constant, so if the project earns more than the after-tax cost of debt, EPS rises — but the higher fixed interest also raises the EPS break-even (the EBIT at which the two financing plans give equal EPS). Equity avoids fixed charges and dilutes EPS now but reduces financial risk. The right answer depends on expected EBIT relative to that indifference point and on preserving bonding capacity.

The EPS/EBIT indifference point

When choosing between a debt plan and an equity plan, the indifference point is the EBIT at which both produce the same earnings per share. Set the two EPS expressions equal: (EBIT − interest)(1 − tax) ÷ shares under each plan. Above that EBIT, the debt plan — with fewer shares — gives higher EPS and leverage works in the owners' favor; below it, the equity plan wins and the fixed interest is a drag. The decision therefore hinges on how confident management is that EBIT will sit comfortably above the indifference point through the cycle. For a contractor whose EBIT swings with the construction cycle, a plan that looks superior at expected EBIT can reverse in a downturn — which is exactly why volatile-cash-flow firms carry less debt.

Combined leverage

Operating and financial leverage compound. The degree of combined leverage (DCL) = DOL × DFL measures how a change in sales flows all the way through to EPS. A contractor with a high operating leverage from its fixed overhead (the DOL computed from CVP in month nine) and a financial leverage of 1.2 here might have a combined leverage of, say, 4.0 × 1.2 = 4.8 — meaning a 10% change in sales swings EPS by roughly 48%. High combined leverage is a double-edged sword: spectacular in an upswing, dangerous in a contraction, and a direct input to how much debt is prudent.

Capital-structure theory

Three frameworks anchor the exam. Modigliani-Miller, without taxes, holds that capital structure is irrelevant to firm value — value comes from the assets, not the financing. Introduce corporate taxes and the interest tax shield makes debt value-adding, pushing toward more leverage. Trade-off theory tempers that: the optimal structure balances the tax-shield benefit of debt against rising costs of financial distress (bankruptcy risk, lost bonding, fire-sale asset values) — there is an interior optimum, not "all debt." Pecking-order theory observes that, because of information asymmetry, firms prefer internal funds first, then debt, and issue equity only as a last resort — which is why a profitable contractor reinvests earnings before borrowing and borrows before selling equity. For MBG, the trade-off optimum is shaped by an extra constraint most firms lack: leverage that threatens the working-capital and equity base also shrinks bonding capacity, so the practical debt ceiling is often tighter than the tax math alone would suggest.

Signaling, agency, and dividend interaction

Capital-structure choices also send signals. Because managers know more than outside investors, issuing equity can be read as a signal that managers think the stock is overpriced — often depressing the price on announcement — while taking on debt signals confidence that future cash flows will cover it. That asymmetry underpins the pecking order. Leverage also has an agency dimension: debt's fixed payments discipline management against wasting free cash flow on empire-building (a benefit), but heavy leverage can tempt owners toward risky "bet the company" projects that shift value from lenders (a cost), which is why lenders impose covenants. Finally, financing and dividend policy interact: paying out earnings reduces internal funds and forces earlier reliance on external capital, while retaining them — the pecking order's first choice — builds the equity and working capital that, for MBG, directly expand bonding capacity. The practical lesson is that the optimal structure is not one number from a formula but a range shaped by taxes, distress costs, signaling, covenants, and, for a contractor, the bonding constraint sitting on top of them all.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR tests the debt-versus-equity trade-off, degree of financial leverage, and the EPS/EBIT indifference logic. The construction wrinkle — working capital and equity drive bonding capacity, which caps revenue — is exactly the kind of industry application BAR rewards. Expect a DFL computation and a question on what happens to ROE and risk as leverage rises.

Practice and recap

  1. Weigh debt versus equity on cost, control, flexibility, and risk.
  2. Compute the degree of financial leverage and interpret the magnification.
  3. Estimate bonding capacity from working capital and the surety multiplier.
  4. Compare financing plans by their effect on EPS and financial risk.

Recap: debt is cheaper but riskier; leverage magnifies returns (MBG's DFL is 1.2); and for a contractor, working capital and equity set the bonding ceiling — roughly $30M aggregate on $3M of working capital — which ultimately caps how much work can be taken.

weeks.title: Working-Capital Management — Cash Conversion, Retainage & Discounts (CMA P2-B · feeds FAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — $400,000.00 sitting idle is a working-capital failure

Real MBG facts: $400,000.00 is stranded across 7 dormant bank accounts, the Q1 payables batch is $284,500.00, and retainage (account 2120) holds back cash on both sides of every job. Working-capital management is about how fast cash moves through the operating cycle and how much is tied up along the way. Idle cash, slow retainage collection, and mis-timed payables all cost real money.

The cash conversion cycle

The cash conversion cycle (CCC) measures the days between paying for inputs and collecting from customers:

CCC = days inventory outstanding + days sales outstanding − days payable outstanding.

For a contractor, "inventory" is work in process (costs in excess of billings). Using month 7's figures: days in WIP = ($1,450,000 ÷ $20,640,000) × 365 = 25.6 days; days sales outstanding = 48.7 days; days payable outstanding = 24.8 days. So CCC = 25.6 + 48.7 − 24.8 = 49.5 days. MBG finances roughly 50 days of operations before cash comes back. Shortening any leg — billing faster, collecting retainage sooner, or paying suppliers later within terms — frees cash.

Cash management — stop stranding cash

The $400,000.00 in dormant accounts is working capital earning nothing and, as month 7 showed, it overstates usable liquidity. Cash management concentrates balances (sweeps), forecasts short-term needs (the 13-week forecast), and invests true surplus in safe, liquid instruments. The goal is enough cash to meet obligations and bonding tests without leaving large idle balances that could retire 28%+ debt or fund bonding-supporting working capital.

Receivables and retainage

Retainage — typically 5–10% withheld until completion — stretches days sales outstanding well beyond normal terms, which is why a contractor's DSO runs high. Managing receivables means disciplined progress billing, prompt lien-waiver and retainage-release administration, and credit evaluation of owners and general contractors. Every day shaved off DSO releases cash one-for-one.

Payables and the cost of forgoing a discount

Paying later within terms is free financing, but skipping an early-payment discount is expensive. The annualized cost of forgoing a discount is:

Cost = [discount % ÷ (100% − discount %)] × [365 ÷ (full period − discount period)].

For terms of 2/10 net 30: [2 ÷ 98] × [365 ÷ (30 − 10)] = 0.0204 × 18.25 = 37.2% annualized. Forgoing a 2/10 discount to hold cash 20 extra days costs about 37% a year — far more than any bank line. Unless MBG is liquidity-constrained, taking the discount is the right call; the discipline is to pay on the net date when no discount is offered, and on the discount date when one is.

Working-capital financing strategy

Firms choose how to fund current assets. A matching (maturity-matching) strategy funds temporary current assets with short-term debt and permanent current assets with long-term capital. An aggressive strategy funds more with short-term debt — cheaper but riskier (refinancing and rate risk). A conservative strategy uses more long-term capital — safer but costlier. For a cyclical contractor, matching protects bonding capacity while controlling cost.

What the cash cycle costs in dollars

The cash conversion cycle is not just a number of days — it is financed working capital that costs real interest. If MBG's roughly 50-day cycle ties up an average of $2,000,000 in net working capital and its short-term financing costs 8%, the cycle costs about $2,000,000 × 8% × (50 ÷ 365) ≈ $22,000 per turn, and it turns several times a year. Shaving ten days off collections does not just "improve a ratio"; it frees cash that either retires high-rate debt or supports more bonded work. That is why receivables and retainage discipline earns its keep.

Managing each component

Cash. Beyond sweeping idle balances, formal models set target cash: the Baumol model treats cash like inventory with a fixed order cost and a holding (interest) cost, while the Miller-Orr model sets upper and lower control limits for firms with uncertain daily flows, returning to a target when a bound is hit. Both answer "how much cash is too much idle versus too little buffer." Receivables. A credit policy weighs the gross margin gained from looser terms against the carrying cost and bad-debt risk; aging schedules and disciplined retainage-release administration are the day-to-day controls. Inventory/materials. The economic-order-quantity logic balances ordering costs against carrying costs; for a builder, just-in-time material delivery reduces carrying cost and site theft but raises the risk of a price spike or a stockout that idles a crew.

Short-term financing and the traps

Temporary needs are funded with a line of credit (revolving, often secured by receivables), trade credit (free within terms), or, more expensively, factoring receivables. Each has a true cost that must be compared on an annualized basis — the same discipline as the cost-of-forgoing-a-discount calculation. The recurring pitfalls: financing permanent working capital with short-term debt (refinancing and rate risk at exactly the wrong moment), letting idle cash accumulate while high-rate debt runs, and treating retainage as collectible on normal terms when it lags months past completion. Working-capital management is where a contractor's interest burden and bonding ceiling are quietly won or lost.

Permanent versus temporary working capital — a worked view

Not all working capital is alike. Permanent working capital is the minimum level a going concern always carries — a base of receivables, materials, and operating cash that never falls to zero — and it behaves like a long-term asset that should be funded with long-term capital. Temporary working capital is the seasonal or project-driven bulge (a busy building season, a large job ramping up) that appropriately rides on short-term financing and unwinds when the work bills out. Mismatching the two is the classic error: funding the permanent base with a revolving line exposes the firm to a credit pull or rate spike at the worst time, while funding the temporary bulge with long-term debt leaves expensive capital idle in the slow season.

Consider a worked receivables decision. Suppose loosening credit terms is expected to add $500,000 of annual contribution margin but raises average receivables by $1,200,000 and adds $40,000 of bad debt. If the carrying cost of the extra receivables is 8%, the total cost is $1,200,000 × 8% + $40,000 = $136,000 — well below the $500,000 of added margin — so the looser policy creates value. Reverse the margin and the answer flips. Every working-capital policy is this kind of trade-off: the benefit of the incremental sale or held inventory against the carrying cost and risk of the assets it creates.

CPA Crossover — FAR

FAR reinforces the classification and measurement behind these items — receivables, retainage, contract assets and liabilities, and the timing that drives the cash cycle. Expect a BAR-style cash-conversion-cycle computation and a classic cost-of-forgoing-a-discount question; both reward exact day counts and the correct formula.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute the cash conversion cycle from days in WIP, DSO, and DPO.
  2. Sweep idle cash; do not let balances sit dormant.
  3. Manage retainage and progress billing to shorten DSO.
  4. Compute the annualized cost of forgoing a discount and decide accordingly.
  5. Match financing maturity to asset permanence.

Recap: MBG's cash conversion cycle is about 49.5 days; idle dormant cash and slow retainage lengthen it, while forgoing a 2/10 net 30 discount costs roughly 37% a year. Working-capital management is where a contractor's liquidity — and therefore its bonding capacity — is won or lost.

weeks.title: Restructuring, M&A & International Finance (CMA P2-B · feeds FAR/BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — MBG already runs an internal capital structure

Real MBG fact: MBG and Riverton are linked by an intercompany note (MBG note receivable 89012 ↔ Riverton note payable 89013), a real example of structuring capital between related entities. This week introduces the strategic-finance topics that sit on top of valuation: mergers and acquisitions, corporate restructuring, and international finance.

Mergers and acquisitions — motives and types

Firms combine to capture synergy — value the combined entity creates beyond the sum of the parts. Types: horizontal (same industry/stage — two general contractors), vertical (supplier or customer — a GC buying a framing sub), and conglomerate (unrelated). Motives include economies of scale, market access, vertical control, tax attributes, and diversification. Not all motives create value; "growth for growth's sake" and empire-building destroy it.

Synergy = value(combined) − [value(A) + value(B)]. Using an illustrative example: MBG standalone value $8,000,000, a target $4,000,000, combined value $13,500,000. Synergy = $13,500,000 − $12,000,000 = $1,500,000. The maximum MBG should pay for the target is its standalone value plus the synergy: $4,000,000 + $1,500,000 = $5,500,000. Paying more transfers all the created value to the seller.

Valuation and consideration

Targets are valued by discounted cash flow (intrinsic), comparable-company multiples, and precedent transactions. For a private target — like most construction firms — multiples and precedent deals carry the weight because there is no market price (the private-company limit from month 7). Consideration can be cash (clean, taxable to the seller, uses the acquirer's liquidity/debt capacity) or stock (shares risk and reward, may defer seller tax, dilutes the acquirer). A deal is accretive if it raises the acquirer's EPS and dilutive if it lowers it.

Corporate restructuring

Restructuring reshapes the asset or capital base: divestitures and spin-offs shed non-core units; recapitalization changes the debt/equity mix; debt restructuring renegotiates terms to relieve distress. For MBG the relevant version is internal: how capital is allocated between entities through the intercompany note and equity, and how those balances eliminate on consolidation (month 7, week 4). Sound intercompany structuring keeps each entity adequately capitalized for its own bonding.

International finance

Cross-border operations add foreign-exchange risk (transaction, translation, and economic — building on ASC 830 from month 7), country/political risk, and transfer-pricing considerations between affiliated entities in different jurisdictions. Firms manage FX exposure with natural hedges (matching foreign revenues and costs) and financial hedges (forwards, options). Transfer prices between related parties must reflect arm's-length pricing for tax compliance — the same intercompany discipline MBG applies to 89010/89011, scaled across borders.

Accretion, dilution, and the acquisition method

When a deal is paid in stock, whether it helps the acquirer's owners turns on a simple comparison the exam loves: a stock-for-stock acquisition is accretive when the acquirer's P/E is higher than the price-to-earnings multiple it pays for the target (so it "buys" cheaper earnings) and dilutive when it pays a higher multiple than its own. A high-multiple buyer acquiring a low-multiple target raises its own EPS purely from the multiple arbitrage; the reverse destroys EPS even if the businesses fit. Cash deals avoid share dilution but consume liquidity and debt capacity. Under the acquisition method (the consolidation accounting from FAR), the buyer records the target's identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, and any excess of purchase price over net identifiable fair value becomes goodwill — an asset tested for impairment, not amortized. A bargain purchase (price below fair value) instead books a gain.

The three foreign-exchange exposures

International operations create three distinct exposures. Transaction exposure is the gain/loss on specific foreign-currency receivables and payables between booking and settlement (the worked euro-equipment loss from month 7, week 4). Translation (accounting) exposure is the effect of restating a foreign subsidiary's statements into the reporting currency — parked in OCI under the current-rate method. Economic (operating) exposure is the deepest: the change in the present value of future cash flows from long-run rate movements that shift competitiveness, even with no foreign-currency transactions on the books. Firms manage these with natural hedges (matching foreign revenues and costs), forwards and futures (lock a rate), options (insure against adverse moves while keeping upside), and currency swaps.

Transfer pricing and country risk

Between affiliated entities across borders, transfer prices must be set at arm's length for tax compliance; accepted methods include the comparable-uncontrolled-price, cost-plus, and resale-price methods. Aggressive transfer pricing to shift income to low-tax jurisdictions invites adjustment and penalties — the same integrity discipline MBG applies to its domestic intercompany accounts, scaled up. Cross-border deals also carry country/political risk (expropriation, capital controls, instability) that is layered into a higher discount rate or mitigated through insurance and financing structure. The recurring traps: confusing accretion with strategic fit (a deal can lift EPS yet destroy value, or create value yet dilute EPS), and ignoring economic exposure because no transaction is denominated in foreign currency.

Synergy types, due diligence, and a worked accretion

Synergies come in identifiable forms, and naming them disciplines the valuation. Revenue synergies (cross-selling, market access) are notoriously optimistic and are discounted heavily by experienced acquirers; cost synergies (eliminating duplicate overhead, purchasing scale) are more reliable; financial synergies (a stronger combined balance sheet, lower cost of capital, usable tax attributes) are real but bounded. Only synergies that are probable and quantifiable should drive the price — paying today for hoped-for revenue synergies is how acquirers overpay.

Due diligence is the safeguard: verifying the target's earnings quality, contingent liabilities, and customer concentration, and — for a contractor target — its WIP schedule, backlog, surety relationships, and the realism of its percentage-of-completion estimates. A target that has been pulling profit forward through aggressive estimates is worth far less than its reported earnings suggest.

A worked accretion check: MBG (illustratively) trades at a 12× price-to-earnings multiple and acquires a target for stock at an effective 9× the target's earnings. Because MBG issues shares worth 12× earnings to buy earnings priced at 9×, the deal adds more earning power per new share than it dilutes — it is accretive. Had it paid 15× for the same earnings, the new shares would carry less earning power than MBG's existing base and the deal would be dilutive, no matter how compelling the strategic story sounded. The number and the narrative must agree before a combination makes sense. For MBG, the same discipline that keeps its intercompany notes balanced to the penny is what should govern any acquisition price: pay for verified value, not for a persuasive story, and let the accretion math veto a deal the strategy slides cannot.

CPA Crossover — FAR / BAR

FAR tests business-combination accounting (acquisition method, goodwill, intercompany eliminations) and foreign-currency standards; BAR tests synergy, valuation multiples, and accretion/dilution. Expect a synergy or maximum-price computation and a question separating accretive from dilutive deals. The intercompany and FX threads here connect directly to month 7, week 4.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify a combination as horizontal, vertical, or conglomerate, and test whether it creates synergy.
  2. Compute synergy and the maximum price a buyer should pay.
  3. Choose cash versus stock consideration and judge accretion/dilution.
  4. Identify FX, country, and transfer-pricing risks in cross-border finance.

Recap: M&A is justified only by real synergy ($1,500,000 in the example, capping the price at $5,500,000); restructuring reshapes the asset and capital base; and international finance layers FX and transfer-pricing risk onto the same intercompany discipline MBG already practices.

weeks.title: CVP Analysis — Breakeven, Margin of Safety & Operating Leverage (CMA P2-C · feeds BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — how many spec homes must MBG close to break even?

Decision analysis is the highest-weighted topic on CMA Part 2 (25%), and cost-volume-profit (CVP) is its foundation. Consider an illustrative MBG spec-home line: average sale price $400,000, variable (direct job) cost $300,000 per home, and annual fixed overhead of $1,800,000 — the same general-and-administrative figure used in months 7 and 8. CVP turns those numbers into the questions an owner actually asks: how many homes to break even, how much cushion exists, and how violently profit swings with volume.

Contribution margin — the engine of CVP

Contribution margin (CM) per unit = price − variable cost = $400,000 − $300,000 = $100,000. It is what each home contributes toward fixed costs and then profit. The contribution-margin ratio = CM ÷ price = $100,000 ÷ $400,000 = 25%. Note CM is not gross margin: CM removes only variable costs, while fixed overhead stays below the line until volume covers it.

Breakeven

Breakeven in units = fixed costs ÷ CM per unit = $1,800,000 ÷ $100,000 = 18 homes. Breakeven in revenue = fixed costs ÷ CM ratio = $1,800,000 ÷ 0.25 = $7,200,000 (which is 18 homes × $400,000, so the two methods agree). Below 18 homes MBG loses money on this line; above it, each additional home drops its full $100,000 CM to operating income.

Target profit

To earn a target operating profit, add it to fixed costs: units for a $300,000 target = ($1,800,000 + $300,000) ÷ $100,000 = 21 homes.

Margin of safety

If MBG expects to close 24 homes, the margin of safety = actual − breakeven = 24 − 18 = 6 homes, or in percentage terms = 6 ÷ 24 = 25%. Sales could fall 25% before the line hits breakeven. Margin of safety is a direct read on how much risk cushion a volume assumption carries.

Operating leverage

Fixed costs create operating leverage: once they are covered, profit accelerates. The degree of operating leverage (DOL) = contribution margin ÷ operating income. At 24 homes: contribution margin = 24 × $100,000 = $2,400,000; operating income = $2,400,000 − $1,800,000 = $600,000; DOL = $2,400,000 ÷ $600,000 = 4.0. A 10% rise in sales lifts operating income by about 40%; a 10% fall cuts it by about 40%. High operating leverage rewards volume and punishes downturns — exactly why a cyclical builder watches its fixed-cost base. (This pairs with the degree of financial leverage from month 8; together they form combined leverage.)

CVP assumptions and limits

CVP assumes a relevant range where price and variable cost per unit are constant and fixed costs are truly fixed, a single product or constant sales mix, and volume as the only cost driver. Real jobs vary in price and cost, and a multi-product mix requires a weighted-average contribution margin. Used within its assumptions, CVP is a fast, powerful screen; pushed outside the relevant range, it misleads.

Multi-product CVP and the sales mix

A real contractor sells more than one thing — spec homes, renovations, small commercial jobs — so single-product breakeven is a simplification. With multiple products, CVP uses a weighted-average contribution margin based on the expected sales mix. Suppose MBG expects to sell three spec homes for every renovation, with home contribution margin $100,000 and renovation contribution margin $40,000. The weighted-average CM per "bundle" of four jobs is (3 × $100,000 + 1 × $40,000) = $340,000 per bundle, or $85,000 per job on average. Breakeven in bundles = fixed cost ÷ bundle CM; multiply back out by the mix to get units of each product. The critical caveat: breakeven holds only at the assumed mix. If the cheaper renovations grow as a share of sales, the weighted-average CM falls and the true breakeven rises — a shift in mix can turn a planned profit into a loss without any change in total volume.

After-tax targets and sensitivity

When a target is stated after tax, gross it up first: required pre-tax profit = after-tax target ÷ (1 − tax rate). A $228,000 after-tax goal at a 24% rate needs $228,000 ÷ 0.76 = $300,000 pre-tax, which then plugs into the target-profit formula — the 21-home answer from the base case. CVP is also a sensitivity tool: because breakeven = fixed ÷ unit CM, a 10% rise in fixed overhead raises breakeven by 10% (18 → ~20 homes), while a price cut that drops unit CM from $100,000 to $90,000 raises breakeven from 18 to 20 homes even with costs unchanged. Walking these one-variable shifts shows management which lever — price, variable cost, fixed cost, or volume — most threatens the plan.

Reading margin of safety and leverage together

Margin of safety and operating leverage are two views of the same risk. A thin margin of safety (sales close to breakeven) always pairs with a high degree of operating leverage, because near breakeven, operating income is small and the ratio of contribution margin to operating income is large. A contractor with heavy fixed equipment and overhead costs lives with high operating leverage: profits scale fast above breakeven and losses scale fast below it, so the margin of safety is the buffer that keeps a normal sales dip from becoming a loss year. This is exactly why bonding and lending analysis (month seven) watches the fixed-cost base — it determines how violently a revenue shortfall hits the bottom line.

Common CVP pitfalls

Three traps recur. First, treating fixed costs as fixed outside the relevant range — step costs such as a second crew or another superintendent jump as volume climbs, so a single linear model breaks past a point. Second, confusing contribution margin with gross margin: gross margin subtracts all product costs including fixed job overhead, while contribution margin subtracts only variable costs, so the two answer different questions and produce different breakevens. Third, ignoring the cash-versus-accrual gap — accounting breakeven is not cash breakeven, because depreciation is a fixed cost in the model but not a cash outflow, so a contractor can sit above accounting breakeven yet run short of cash when receivables and retainage lag. Each pitfall turns a clean CVP chart into a misleading one, which is why the assumptions deserve as much scrutiny as the arithmetic. A fourth, subtler trap is assuming a constant sales mix in a multi-product setting: the weighted-average contribution margin — and therefore breakeven — silently changes the moment the mix shifts toward lower-margin work, so the single breakeven figure must be re-derived whenever the expected mix moves, not carried forward as if it were a fixed property of the business.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR tests breakeven in units and dollars, target-profit volume, margin of safety, and the degree of operating leverage, plus the trap of confusing contribution margin with gross margin. Expect a question where you must compute DOL and translate a percentage sales change into a percentage profit change.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute CM per unit and the CM ratio.
  2. Find breakeven in units and in revenue.
  3. Solve for target-profit volume.
  4. Compute margin of safety in units and percent.
  5. Compute the degree of operating leverage and interpret it.

Recap: with a $100,000 contribution margin and $1,800,000 of fixed cost, MBG's spec-home line breaks even at 18 homes ($7,200,000); at 24 homes the margin of safety is 25% and the degree of operating leverage is 4.0, so profit moves four times as fast as sales.

weeks.title: Relevant-Cost Analysis — Make-or-Buy, Special Orders, Sell-or-Process (CMA P2-C)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — should MBG self-perform framing or subcontract it?

Every contractor faces the make-or-buy choice constantly: run its own crew or hire a sub. The exam answers it with relevant-cost analysis — consider only costs that are future and that differ between the alternatives. Sunk costs and unavoidable allocated overhead are irrelevant, no matter how large they look on the job sheet.

What makes a cost relevant

A relevant cost is a future cash flow that changes with the decision. Sunk costs (already incurred — engineering already paid, land already bought) are never relevant. Unavoidable allocated fixed overhead that continues regardless of the choice is not relevant. Opportunity cost — the contribution given up by using a resource one way instead of another — is relevant even though it never appears in the ledger.

Make-or-buy — self-perform versus subcontract

Consider an illustrative framing scope. Self-performing has avoidable costs of direct labor $120,000, employer burden $40,000, and avoidable variable overhead $20,000 = $180,000. A separate $30,000 of allocated fixed overhead continues whether or not MBG self-performs, so it is irrelevant. The subcontractor bid is $200,000.

Compare only the relevant amounts: self-perform $180,000 versus subcontract $200,000. If the crew has idle capacity, self-performing saves $20,000. But suppose that crew could otherwise earn $35,000 of contribution on another job — that is an opportunity cost. Now self-perform costs $180,000 + $35,000 = $215,000, which exceeds the $200,000 subcontract bid, so subcontracting becomes the better choice. The decision flips entirely on whether capacity is truly idle.

Special orders

A special order at a price below normal can still be profitable if there is idle capacity and it will not spoil regular pricing. Accept when the price exceeds the relevant (incremental) cost, usually variable cost plus any incremental fixed cost. Illustrative: a one-off small job has incremental cost of $250,000 and is offered at $280,000. With idle capacity, accepting adds $30,000 of contribution — take it. If accepting would displace full-price work or require new fixed capacity, those effects enter the relevant calculation and can reverse the answer.

Sell-or-process-further

When an asset can be sold as-is or improved and sold for more, the joint or original cost is sunk and irrelevant. Decide on the incremental revenue versus incremental cost of processing further. Illustrative: a graded lot sells now for $90,000; with $25,000 of additional site work it sells for $130,000. Incremental revenue $40,000 exceeds incremental cost $25,000, so process further for a $15,000 gain. The original land cost does not enter the decision at all.

Structuring the analysis and the qualitative side

The discipline that prevents errors is to lay the decision out as a differential analysis: list every cost and revenue, mark which ones change between the alternatives, and total only those. A make-or-buy schedule shows the avoidable costs of self-performing (direct labor, burden, avoidable variable and fixed overhead, opportunity cost of the capacity) in one column and the subcontract price plus any added purchasing or inspection cost in the other; the unavoidable allocated overhead appears in neither because it does not change. Building the schedule the same way every time keeps sunk and allocated costs from sneaking in.

Qualitative factors can override the numbers. Self-performing keeps control of quality, schedule, and crew know-how, and preserves the trade skills that win future work; subcontracting frees capacity for higher-value jobs and shifts performance risk to the sub — but it depends on the sub's reliability and exposes MBG to the sub's failures on a bonded project. A decision that is marginally cheaper to outsource may still be wrong if it hollows out a core capability or jeopardizes a critical schedule.

Special orders under a capacity constraint

The simple special-order rule — accept if price exceeds incremental cost — assumes idle capacity. When the firm is at capacity, accepting a special order means giving up other work, so the analysis must add the opportunity cost of the displaced full-price job. A special job priced at $280,000 with $250,000 of incremental cost looks profitable in isolation, but if taking it bumps a regular job that would have contributed $50,000, the true comparison is $30,000 of special-order contribution against $50,000 forgone — reject it. The same special order can be a clear accept with idle crews and a clear reject when the schedule is full.

Joint products and the split-off point

When one process yields multiple products, the joint cost incurred before the split-off point is sunk and irrelevant to any sell-or-process-further decision; only the incremental revenue and cost beyond split-off matter. Allocating joint cost across products (by physical units or relative sales value) is required for inventory valuation but must never drive a process-further decision — a product can look unprofitable after a full joint-cost allocation yet still be worth processing because its incremental revenue exceeds its incremental cost. The recurring traps across all relevant-cost problems are the same three: importing sunk costs, importing unavoidable allocated overhead, and forgetting opportunity cost when capacity binds.

Outsourcing as a recurring strategic decision

Make-or-buy is not a one-time calculation but a standing strategic posture. A contractor that self-performs concrete, framing, and finish carpentry holds tighter control of schedule and quality and keeps its crews busy between bid wins, but it carries the fixed payroll and equipment of those trades through slow periods. A contractor that subcontracts broadly converts fixed cost to variable, scales up and down with the backlog, and shifts performance risk to subs — at the price of thinner margins, dependence on sub availability, and exposure to a sub's default on a bonded job. The relevant-cost math sets the floor for any single scope, but the standing decision also weighs capacity for higher-value work, the strategic importance of owning a capability, and the reliability of the subcontractor market. The exam-tested core stays constant: decide on incremental, future, differential cash flows, add opportunity cost whenever a resource is constrained, and let the qualitative factors break a tie the numbers leave close.

A useful discipline is to evaluate outsourcing on total cost of ownership rather than the headline subcontract price: add the cost of selecting and managing the sub, inspecting the work, carrying the risk of rework or a missed schedule, and the certificate-of-insurance and lien-waiver administration the relationship demands. Conversely, an insourcing decision should count the cost of recruiting and retaining the trade, the equipment and its maintenance, and the idle-time cost in slow periods. The cheapest-looking option on a single scope can be the most expensive once these wrap-around costs are included, which is why the differential schedule should reach beyond the obvious labor-versus-bid comparison to the full set of cash flows each path actually triggers.

CPA Crossover — decision analysis

These relevant-cost patterns appear across CMA and BAR alike. The reliable traps are (1) including sunk costs, (2) including unavoidable allocated fixed overhead, and (3) forgetting opportunity cost when capacity is constrained. Build the analysis from incremental cash flows only.

Practice and recap

  1. Keep only future, differential cash flows; drop sunk costs and unavoidable allocated overhead.
  2. Compare avoidable self-perform cost to the subcontract price.
  3. Add opportunity cost when the resource has an alternative use.
  4. Accept a special order when price exceeds incremental cost and capacity is idle.
  5. Decide sell-or-process on incremental revenue versus incremental cost; ignore the sunk joint cost.

Recap: relevant-cost analysis self-performs the framing for a $20,000 saving when capacity is idle, but subcontracts once a $35,000 opportunity cost is counted. Only future, differential cash flows decide.

weeks.title: Pricing Decisions & Target Costing — How MBG Bids a Job (CMA P2-C · feeds BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — markup on cost is not the same as margin on price

MBG bids work two ways: build the price up from cost (cost-plus) or start from what the market will pay and design the cost down to fit (target costing). The single most common pricing error — on the exam and on real bids — is confusing a markup on cost with a margin on price. This week makes the distinction precise and computes both, plus the target-costing discipline.

Cost-plus (markup on cost)

Markup on cost applies a percentage to the job cost. With an illustrative job cost of $300,000 and a 20% markup: bid = $300,000 × (1 + 0.20) = $360,000. The $60,000 markup is 20% of cost but only $60,000 ÷ $360,000 = 16.7% of the price. Cost-plus is simple and common in change orders and time-and-materials work, but it does not guarantee the market will accept the price.

Margin on price

A target margin on price is solved differently: price = cost ÷ (1 − margin). To earn a 20% margin on price from the same $300,000 cost: price = $300,000 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = $300,000 ÷ 0.80 = $375,000. Notice it is higher than the $360,000 from a 20% markup on cost — because 20% of the (larger) price is more dollars than 20% of cost. To earn a 25% margin on price: $300,000 ÷ 0.75 = $400,000, the spec-home price from week 1. Always confirm whether a percentage is stated on cost or on price.

Target costing — design to cost

Target costing reverses the logic: start with the price the market sets, subtract the required profit, and the remainder is the cost the product must hit.

Target cost = target price − required profit.

Illustrative: the market price is $400,000 and MBG requires a 15% margin = $60,000. Target cost = $400,000 − $60,000 = $340,000. If the current expected cost is $360,000, MBG must engineer $20,000 out of the design — value engineering, supplier negotiation, scope or method changes — before committing. Target costing pushes cost discipline to the design stage, where most cost is locked in, rather than discovering an overrun after the slab is poured.

Other pricing considerations

Bid pricing also weighs competition, capacity (a busy contractor bids higher), strategic value of the client, and risk. Change-order pricing follows the contract's agreed markup on added cost and is a major profit lever — disciplined change-order documentation and pricing recover costs that would otherwise erode margin. Predatory or below-cost pricing carries legal and reputational risk and is generally avoided.

Three pricing approaches and the product life cycle

Pricing methods sit on a spectrum. Cost-based pricing (cost-plus, the markup math above) is simple and defensible for cost-reimbursable and change-order work but ignores what the market will bear. Market-based pricing starts from competitors and the customer's alternatives — essential in competitive bidding, where the low responsible bid often wins. Value-based pricing sets price from the value delivered to the customer (speed, quality, a guaranteed completion date), and captures the most margin when the contractor can differentiate. Most real bids blend all three: a cost floor, a market ceiling, and a value-based position in between.

New offerings also follow a life-cycle choice between skimming (a high introductory price to capture early high-value buyers, then lower it) and penetration (a low price to win share quickly and deter entrants). Skimming suits a differentiated or capacity-constrained builder; penetration suits a commoditized market where volume and scale matter.

Elasticity and the legal guardrails

Price elasticity of demand governs how far price can move: where demand is elastic (many substitutes, price-sensitive owners), a price increase loses more volume than it gains in margin, so the profit-maximizing move is often to hold or cut; where demand is inelastic (a specialized, time-critical, or sole-qualified job), there is room to price for value. An analyst pairs elasticity with the contribution margin to find the price that maximizes total contribution, not just the highest price the market will tolerate.

Pricing is also legally bounded: predatory pricing (below cost to drive out competitors), price fixing with competitors, and certain forms of price discrimination between buyers can violate competition law. And target costing closes the loop on all of it — if the market price is fixed at $400,000 and the firm requires a $60,000 margin, the $340,000 target cost is non-negotiable, so the lever shifts from price to cost engineering: value engineering the design, renegotiating supplier terms, or changing methods until the cost fits the price the market has already set.

Contract structures and a worked pricing trade-off

How a contractor is paid shapes the pricing decision. A fixed-price (lump-sum) contract puts cost-overrun risk on MBG, so the bid must build in contingency and the markup math must be conservative. A cost-plus contract (cost plus a fee — fixed fee, or a percentage) shifts cost risk to the owner and rewards documented cost, which is why owners cap it and audit it. A guaranteed-maximum-price contract blends the two, with shared savings below the cap. The pricing method follows the structure: cost-plus and change orders use cost-based markups, while competitive lump-sum work is market-driven with a value-based edge where MBG can differentiate.

A worked trade-off shows why elasticity matters. Suppose at $400,000 MBG expects to sell 24 homes (contribution $100,000 each, total $2,400,000), and a 10% price cut to $360,000 raises volume to 30 homes but drops contribution to $60,000 each — total contribution $1,800,000. Despite selling more, the price cut destroys $600,000 of contribution because demand was not elastic enough to offset the thinner margin. Run the same numbers with a jump to 45 homes and the cut would pay off. The point is that price changes must be evaluated on total contribution, never on volume or revenue alone.

Finally, a contractor's pricing discipline includes the bid/no-bid decision itself. Preparing a competitive bid is costly, and chasing work that is mispriced, outside core competence, or likely to go to a lower-cost competitor wastes estimating capacity that could win better jobs. The same relevant-cost thinking applies: bid when the expected contribution, weighted by the probability of winning, exceeds the cost of bidding and the opportunity cost of the capacity the job would consume. Pricing, in other words, starts before the number is set — with the choice of which work to price at all.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR tests both pricing directions and especially the markup-versus-margin distinction, plus target-cost computation. Expect a question that gives a margin "on sales" and tempts you to apply it as a markup on cost — the wrong answer by design.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute a cost-plus bid as cost × (1 + markup).
  2. Compute a price for a target margin as cost ÷ (1 − margin).
  3. Distinguish markup on cost from margin on price every time.
  4. Compute target cost as price − required profit and size the gap to close.

Recap: a 20% markup on a $300,000 cost bids $360,000, while a 20% margin on price requires $375,000 and a 25% margin requires $400,000. Target costing works backward from a $400,000 market price to a $340,000 target cost, demanding $20,000 of design savings.
